maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY FUNDING
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should
consider the advisability of reinstating funding for the Canadian
Centre for Occupational Health and Safety.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of privilege that I rise in this House today on my motion which calls upon Parliament to urge the federal government to reinstate funding for the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety located in Hamilton, Ontario.
At the outset of this debate I would like to thank the members of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges, Procedures and Private Members' Business for allowing this motion to become a votable item. I believe the decision shows not only the strength of this motion but the strength of parliamentary reform as well.
This motion speaks for all Canadians. While the Conservative government slashes through what it sees as the jungle of needless public expense, the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, the CCOHS, is headed for disaster. For ten years the federal government has made a wise business decision by investing in the CCOHS.
Through its preventative role, the centre has saved the federal government, Canadians, millions of dollars a year in health care costs.
According to a poll carried out for The Toronto Star and CTV, Canadians strongly oppose reductions for, among other things, health and education. However, instead of investing in Canadians, in their health and in their future, the Conservative government is divesting itself of what is rightly its responsibility.
The CCOHS was established by Act of Parliament in 1979, as a national institute concerned with the study, encouragement and co-operative advancement of occupational health and safety. The centre has traditionally provided Canadians and the international community with cost-free, impartial and unbiased information on occupational health and safety matters in both official languages. Through the use of its telephone hotline services, technical publications and on-line computer data bases, people can obtain information from the centre virtually trouble free.
The important and valuable role of the centre is obvious. Occupational hazards rank as the number three cause of death to Canadians, right behind heart disease and cancer. Compared to the U.S., Japan, West Germany and Great Britain, Canada has the highest rate of fatalities due to occupational hazards. In 1987, 894 Canadians died as a result of occupational accidents; 25 million person days were lost as a result of work related accidents and injuries.
The Minister of Labour acknowledged in the House of Commons that work related accidents entail direct and indirect cost to Canadians in the amount of $17.5 billion a year. Considering the dividends to the Canadian economy in preventing such occupational related accidents, Canadians cannot afford to lose such a valuable institution. Clearly, public funding of the centre has illustrated that old axiom, "An ounce of prevention for a pound of cure".
The responsibility of the centre in providing accurate and non-biased information to Canadians is becoming increasingly important. In 1988-1989, the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety received over 26,000 requests concerning hazardous chemicals. A

February 5, 1990

significant number of these enquiries was received immediately after the PCB fire in St. Basile le Grand, Quebec, from Canadians concerned about the effects of PCBs and other dangerous chemicals.
To give you an idea of the centre's workload, last year alone the CCOHS provided Canadians and the world with over 350,000 copies of 1,000 different technical publications and over 1,200 Canadian companies connected with the centre's computer over 40,000 times.
However, the fuel which drives the centre, that vast pool of information which it provides may soon dry up. Much of the information which the centre disseminates to the public is provided free of charge by international business, foreign governments and the United Nation's World Health Organization and Environmental Program as well as the International Labour Organization.
Because the centre's core funding was slashed in last year's budget and will be completely withdrawn by April of next year, the centre has already resorted to user fees in order to keep itself afloat. The introduction of user fees across the board has wide ranging implications for both the public and for the benevolent organizations which provide information through the centre.
In order to survive in the long-term, the centre's council of governors has established a business plan which would see the introduction of user fees in virtually every case and would redirect the centre's efforts toward the search for new products and services. There is little doubt that user fees would soon turn a profit for the CCOHS. However, I urge this House to recognize today that those profits will just as soon destroy the credibility of this organization, making its role in the promotion of health and safety of workers virtually useless. In many ways this shift to the profit motive will sound the death-knell of this important national institution.
The problems associated with user fees are not only in relation to the worker but to the various bodies which supply information to the centre. User fees may discourage benevolent organizations from supplying information to the centre. Only a small portion of the centre's data bases are actually developed by the centre itself.
Most of the centre's information is derived from a mixture of national and international organizations which have a direct interest in the free flow of information in occupational health and safety matters. Some of these organizations have not yet been informed of this plan by the CCOHS to charge for their information.
One of the centre's contributors, the International Labour Organization, has shown concern that it has not been involved or informed of the desire to introduce user fees for information which, in many cases, is supplied free of charge. In fact, most of the information from which data bases have been created is provided free of charge by the goodwill and commitment of these non-governmental agencies.
The question I would like to address today and which must be asked is what would the willingness of these non-governmental organizations be in providing cost-free information to the centre once they learn that the CCOHS is projected to make millions of dollars from their goodwill and commitment. In addition, the U.S. Congress has questioned the level of involvement which its equivalent, the National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety, should have in providing information to the CCOHS if the centre in turn charges its customers for it.
The implication of user fees is greatest for those whom the centre was first established, the Canadian worker. User fees essentially violate the right of Canadians to access to information on potentially life-threatening situations, free of financial barriers. As the Council of Governors state in their draft business plan:
The centre must become a commercial organization while
operating under its basic mandate of serving workers.
In my opinion the two are not compatible as any reduction in services will, in turn, affect Canadians through a reduction in accessible information. One can only imagine that under a profit-driven business plan it would not be safety that would be the first concern but the edict of the Conservative government itself; the bottom line. The proposed business plan which the Minister of Labour was to receive on January 31 of this year calls for the introduction of new services and projects. Heavy emphasis is placed on the marketing of existing products and services. A portion of the business
February 5, 1990

plan blatantly exposes the intention of the Conservative government. I will quote from that plan:
Based on the belief that the centre has the capability of increasing its existing revenues and -new revenue sources, the Minister of Labour announced -that funding to the centre will be-completely eliminated. The centre has been mandated by the minister to develop a business plan that will show how-the centre will achieve selfsufficiency through the sale of products and services.
I believe this statement illustrates the new philosophy being forced upon the centre. There is no mention of finding the proper balance between self-sufficiency and the rights of the worker to know.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House the following section of the business plan which is a case in point regarding the way in which the centre is evolving. Under the section entitled "Strategies" the draft plan states:
The centre's strategy will be to favour the sale of products as opposed to the delivery of services, because of the revenue generation that can be achieved through products. Once the investment in product development is made, the profit potential is far greater than for services, which require far greater commitment of human resources and generally offer low profit margins.
There you have it, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Profits before health.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY FUNDING
speechtext:
Exactly. Profits before health. The centre, originally established as an institution to help people and to promote occupational health and safety, will now focus on the bottom line and promote its products. The draft plan goes on to explain that a lucrative market for safety-related products exists and that the centre should focus greater energy and resources on developing products and services for sale.
Other aspects of the business plan include a subscription service on occupational health and safety matters targeted at small and medium sized businesses and to develop new and existing markets for the data base information.
The problem I foresee in relation to this business plan is the direction the CCOHS must take under such a market-driven philosophy. The plan will compromise the centre's mandate to promote occupational health and
Private Members' Business
safety in the workplace in Canada and the physical and mental health of working Canadians.
It is the worker who, in the end result, will be compromised by the centre's drive for new products and new services. Surely the Conservative government must be aware that not everything could or should be privatized, especially with regard to the health and safety of workers.
The CCOHS will not be able to serve the very people it was mandated to reach, if, instead, it must apply its energies to potential buyers and potential suppliers of data bases. Worse, Mr. Speaker, those willing to pay the highest price could find their information and their ideas privileged at the expense of the health and safety of workers.
Workers deserve a more objective, arm's length, voice in the selection and distribution of the information, not on the basis of the highest bidder but on the basis of real concern for health and safety in the workplace.
On top of all this is the fact that for all of the new plans and the charges the centre expects to raise, the figure hidden behind it all is that ever present goods and services tax. Under the proposals in the technical paper the centre would have to charge the GST on all of their products making the cost of communicating with the centre just that much farther out of reach for small businesses and the individual labourer.
I would like to note that the total advertising budget for the GST, even before the tax comes into effect, would pay for the operation of the centre for an entire year. Is this what the government means by deficit reduction or wasteful expense? In essence, the CCOHS of tomorrow will be entirely different from the CCOHS of today. It will be profit-driven. Canadian workers will come second to the centre's obsession with marketing and pricing. It will seek the bottom line. It will become complacent as opposed to being on the leading edge of occupational health and safety measures.
The elimination of public funding will jeopardize the tripartite relationship of the centre. This relationship has been the backbone of the centre. The credibility of the CCOHS depends on the trusting relationship between business, government and labour.
Now that the CCOHS is faced with relying on private financing, labour has stated that it does not want to be part of a new commercial operation concerned with

February 5, 1990
Private Members' Business
profit more than safety. As the vice-president of the Canadian Labour Congress stated:
We are only talking about $10 million a year to provide occupational health and safety to all Canadians. That is the job of a federal government, to protect the citizens of the country. If this plan goes ahead, I do not think we are going to have any choice but to withdraw our support from the centre.
This will mean that user fees will hurt those people the centre was designed to protect. Because of the cost to small companies and workers without unions user fees will discourage inquiries leaving business to provide their employees with safety information.
Many critics have argued that placing the burden on small businesses and labour is scrimping on a false economy. One expert in the occupational health and safety field recently stated:
The direct savings contributed by the centre could be estimated at more than three times its budget. This centre is already paying for itself hundreds of times over every year. The government now says that due to the national debt, the centre must find alternative financing. It will save $10 million a year by cutting off subsidies to the centre. Simple arithmetic shows that the real cost if the centre closes will probably run into hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
Simple arithmetic also shows that the government could and should pay for the centre's operations by cutting needless expenses elsewhere. For example, the federal Department of Public Works directed the purchase of a facility for a customs and excise training facility even though Customs and excise said that the facility in question did not suit their purposes. The facility, located in the federal riding of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, was purchased for $5 million.
As the Auditor General stated in his recent annual report to Parliament:
In our opinion, the initial contracts did not provide for a realistic evaluation before the decision to proceed. When construction began in 1986, it was to meet needs established in 1976 and not re-examined since then. Although the consultant's report stated the property would be adequate-with some renovations-the cost of renovations has so far been $35 million.
The Auditor General also describes the fact that there are many loopholes existing in the income tax system which the government could close. These loopholes amount to some $350 million in lost revenue every year. For a government that preaches fiscal responsibility, it would be easier to support measures that would save on
needless expenses, but not on cost-saving institutions such as the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety.
In short, the CCOHS needs public support in order to fulfil its mandate. Under the proposed plan Canadian workers would be compromised by the centre's desire for stability and profit.
Canadian workers need adequate information regarding workplace hazards. We know that. The fact remains that if the centre is unable to survive, if workers and small businesses cannot afford to contact the centre regarding workplace hazards, the real loss will be to the Canadian taxpayer and Canadian workers.
So I am asking my colleagues on all sides of this House to seriously consider my proposal urging that the federal government reinstate funding for the Canadian Centre of Occupational Health and Safety.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak to the motion of my colleague for Hamilton West. I know that he has long had an interest in his community and that he is veiy interested in the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, as he should be. The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety is a tremendous organization. It has proven itself over the last 10 or 12 years as it has developed an excellent record in the dissemination of important information in the field of health.
The information that the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety receives, as the member for Hamilton West mentioned, comes from other organizations. However, he forgot to say that the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety puts that information into a form that Canadian workers and employers can understand it and puts it to use in a very efficient way. The member speaks of this important information and then talks about profit. It will be a long time before there will be profit because even though this is a tripartite government organization the federal government or the taxpayers have been paying almost the full load for the operation of the centre; over $67 million over the last 10 or 12 years. That is a substantial investment.
There are other players, other people at the table in this tripartite organization that governs the centre. The centre does operate autonomously, it makes its own
February 5, 1990

decisions and it develops without being told what to do by the government.
It has built up a tremendous reputation, as the member for Hamilton West indicated. But there comes a time under good fiscal management when the government and also the board of governors believes that there should be some cost recovery developed into a plan. And the centre has been doing that over the last number of years consistently, albeit slowly. The federal government believes that that should be accelerated to a certain extent and so we have said that the centre should move into more of a cost-recovery mode and it has now developed a plan to look at doing so.
As a result of receiving government funding only-although it had a good reputation and did a good job-I think that a lot of people did not know what the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety did. There are a lot of school boards and fire departments and so on which did not know. I see the member opposite from northern Ontario. I am sure he knows about it because he was involved in assisting workers.
Were we really spreading the word? As a result of not having to worry about where the funding comes from there may have been a less than an adequate job done on that. The business plan that is just now being developed will have to do an even better job with the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety by spreading the word and being helpful in a much better way.
The member opposite indicated that NIOSH and other organizations would not continue to give the centre information because it is moving into a cost-recovery mode. He used the word "profit". I use "cost-recovery" because the discussions that the centre has had with those contributory organizations have indicated that it was in a cost-recovery, or pay-for-the-cost, situation. They have no trouble with that at all.
I might be very surprised about what the International Labour Organization thinks about this very important plan. I think the plan is very exciting. It looks at the opportunities for the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety to spread out, to move. It has been mainly concentrated on the health side, as I think
Private Members' Business
members opposite who are interested know. It will now have the opportunity to move in a much more direct way into the safety side. Members will agree that it has been mainly operating on the health side and not as aggressively and helpfully on the safety side as it perhaps could be. I see that developing under this important business plan that has been brought forward.
We want the centre to carry on and expand. My colleague from Hamilton West mentioned that the centre is going to have to move into new product development. What is wrong with that? I think it is absolutely great that it is going to move into new product development. It will be putting on leadership seminars and conferences, as is proposed in the plan, as well as moving most certainly and directly toward becoming a self-sustaining organization, first, in connection with the CCINFO disc, that tremendous technology which it has that gives so much information to the worker and the employer. It will carry on from there developing new products and getting into conferences and seminars.
The cost projection is nothing tremendous. It looks like a 70 per cent or 80 per cent cost increase over the next few years on the CCINFO disc side. However, as is stated in the business plan, the centre will ensure that certain services will continue to be provided at no charge to clients so as not to impose barriers to access to information by individuals across the country. This will also act as a tool to assist the centre in marketing other products and services.
The person who phones for information will receive that information and get a publication and/or data sent immediately. That is what the minister and the government have committed themselves to.
So I look forward to great things. There is certainly great support for the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety on the government side. I have visited it a number of times and as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour I have had close contact with this centre since last May. I know it is going to continue and I know the member opposite for Hamilton West wants that to happen too. We will all work together so that this centre can carry on with its good work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise today in support of the motion put forward by my friend for Hamilton West. The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety was established in 1978. It was established to supply crucial research and information, which is duplicated nowhere else, to all workers in this great country.
It is very obvious to us on this side of the House that the government has a very blatant plan to privatize the CCOHS. In order to privatize an industry you must have a product to sell. In this case, Mr. Speaker, the product is information, information that relates to the health and safety of all workers across Canada. The information is contained on a computer disc which the government tells us can be sold at a high price. And that is what this is all about, profit line.
This is information which was donated and shared by institutes like NIOHS in the United States. Therefore this government is proposing, not only to sell something that we do not own to begin with but also to increase the price of the service.
I listened with interest to the member opposite when he said that it is not profits, it is cost recovery. That kind of says the something to me-the bottom line. I wonder at times why it is that whenever we talk about health and safety in the workplace we have to say "profits" or "cost recovery" in the same breath. Surely somewhere down the line we have to put the health and the safety of our workers before profits.
The member opposite and the government are saying that employers are paying millions of dollars in contributions to these services. I must point out that workers are paying with their health and their lives. When we can offer a service that will educate them so that they know more about what they are working with and what the ramifications are of working with these products, I think this is more in line with what we really want to offer our workers.
We hear it said that we have done well in the health related issues and now we have to look at the safety related issues. Every time I have talked to someone in the business industry about safety the first thing that is said is that it is the worker's fault, he was not paying
attention, or the worker was hung over. It worries me when we talk about safety in that context.
The government has to make a commitment to workers to maintain the CCOHS to ensure that workers and their representatives have free access to this information. If we insist on privatizing this service, which is exactly what we are doing, we are taking that right away from them.
I urge all members of this House to disregard what was said by the other side and support this motion by our friend for Hamilton West.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the chance to speak on this important question today for two reasons. The first is that the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety is a very important institution in this country and an institution to which this government is fully committed.
The second reason is that the chairman, Maureen Shaw, is a constituent of mine from the beautiful southern Alberta foothills. She established credentials in this field over a period of several years and she now commutes to Hamilton at great personal sacrifice to provide able leadership for the centre in this challenging time.
In the past decade the number of occupational accidents and illnesses in Canada has continued to be a major concern to employers, to workers and to all levels of government. In this period of time we have witnessed an increasing willingness and capacity on the part of organizations of employers, workers and governments to co-operate in efforts to reduce these losses, both in terms of human suffering and economic losses. We must increase our efforts and continue to work together to ensure a safe and healthy working environment for all Canadians.
Today we face enormous challenges in the area of occupational health and safety. Fortunately we are equipped with an information centre that was envisaged some 12 years ago by the three social partners in order to meet the future challenges which are now upon us. I am referring, of course, to the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety which was created by an act of Parliament in 1978.
Since its formation the CCOHS has worked towards the objective of reducing the number of occupational accidents and illnesses in Canadian workplaces and has become an increasingly important component of this activity throughout Canada. Within its mandate it has
February 5, 1990

assumed the role of being a national information resource on occupational health and safety matters. The CCOEIS gathers, evaluates and distributes occupational health and safety information to all decision-makers; workers, unions, management, governments and professionals in the field.
The CCOHS information and advisory service answers inquiries from any source about workplace health and safety and related matters. It has developed automated databases on occupational health and safety topics which permit direct access by federal-provincial and territorial government agencies, employers and unions from any part of Canada.
The current economy in Canada dictates a critical need to reduce government deficits and to improve productivity and efficiency. The need to compete internationally also highlights and adds impetus to greater productivity and efficiency. All levels of governments in Canada are finding it necessary to restrain some of their services and some of their programs.
My friend opposite, the hon. member for Hamilton West, referred to a CTV-Toronto Star poll released just last evening. Unlike my hon. colleague, I have no desire to suggest that we should base all public policy on polling data. However, he will have noted also that a huge majority of Canadians also support cutting money going to Crown corporations. The bottom line is that all sectors in society must tighten the belt.
Concerns for rising costs of Worker's Compensation Board programs and of health care in Canada, and the concurrent concern for improving the health status of Canadians, are focusing attention on health promotion, disease prevention and accident prevention.
Occupational safety and health in Canada is a complex field. It embodies a combination of economic, scientific and ethical issues. The field is further complicated by the fact that it is regulated by 13 different occupational safety and health agencies across the country. The importance of this field in Canada and in other countries is becoming increasingly recognized because of the impact of economic, social, technological and demographic trends in this area of activity. It is also recognized
Private Members' Business
because of the impact of trends related to the working environment and to the health field in general.
The impact that these trends are having on the field of occupational safety and health is also opening many opportunities for the CCOHS in performing its mandate. The rising awareness and understanding of health, occupational and general environmental issues is generating an increasing demand for information on these subject areas.
Perhaps the biggest problem facing people who need information in this field is the fact that there is so much information. There is so much that it is very difficult to find that piece of information which is useful to a particular user when they need it.
The CCINFO is the Canadian centre's computerized information service. It provides fast and user-friendly answers to a wide spectrum of occupational health and safety questions. It is also available on-line, the CCINFO line, through a telecommunications link to the central computer at CCOHS. A telephone link also provides user support as well.
The disc, read-only memory, is for microcomputers. It includes data bases, publications and videotex packages in a new application of current technology that requires only a microcomputer to access a very large volume of information. The set of information discs now comprise three discs; two contain chemical information and a third contains occupational health and safety information.
I would like to give hon. members a better appreciation of the capacity of this innovative product. The computer literate members of the House will know that one single three and a half inch compact disc could contain the entire copy of the departmental estimates tabled in this House last spring. A single compact disc can hold up to 300,000 pages of information. So, the application of this technology to the proceedings of this House could contain Hansard and the Canada Gazette would also be a very useful source of information for researchers.
Labour Canada, in conjunction with the centre, has developed a special application compact disc containing federal legislation and standards. This disc is currently undergoing operational trials in Labour Canada and after two to three months it will probably be put into full operation. Labour Canada currently is considering broadening the usefulness of this new tool to incorporate

February 5, 1990
Private Members' Business
operational program directives on the disc and to explore an application in computer-assisted training.
Other federal departments are also exploiting the use of this innovative product which permits gains in efficiency within their own operations. For example, environmental protection, as we all know, is a major concern to Canadians. The effective implementation of environmental protection measures requires partnership among a number of sectors in the Canadian mosaic. This partnership will help preserve and protect the environment by the co-operative contribution of abilities and knowledge. A joint venture between Environment Canada and the centre includes a joint presentation at the Globe 90 exposition planned for Vancouver this upcoming March and will focus on this unique CCOHS information system and complex chemical information.
A direct indicator of the success of this innovative product of the centre is the peer acclaim for its quality and demand, both domestically and internationally, which demonstrates its utility. Several Ontario universities recently approached the centre to resolve a problem related to management of collections of material safety data sheets for the system in many different locations. The CCINFO database responded to this identified special need. These are just some examples of the kinds of products that can be developed in a new and reinvigorated centre.
Both the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Chemical Producers Association have assisted in the development of the CCINFO database for several years. They have also actively promoted the database among their member firms. This encouragement has included establishing the database as a voluntary central repository of material safety data sheets from manufacturers and suppliers of chemicals and by encouraging their member firms to use the database for such related information.
The CCINFO disc has also recently received accolades from Yale University. Yale's medical library in a detailed review of the disc, called it an information resource that is global in scope.
In addition, as a further demonstration of its wide acceptance and marketability, the centre recently signed
an agreement with Geneva-based International Occupational Safety and Health Information Centre, an arm of the ILO, the International Labour Organization. This agreement strongly boosts the centre's ability to market the CCINFO product internationally in Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin America. The centre has excelled in the performance of its mandate and in the information services provided to Canadians at a very low cost.
I wish to assure the House that the centre will continue in its role as a disseminator of occupational health and safety information in Canada. The government will continue to support the centre in its mandate and its role of performing this important service for the benefit of all Canadians. The government is simply asking that other sponsoring partners and the beneficiaries of the centre accept and shoulder their share of the responsibility for funding the centre.
It is a uniquely Canadian institution, created by Canadians to reflect the needs of the country, its industrial milieu and the people of this country. It has been given the task to provide specific occupational health and safety functions and services within a climate of increasing fiscal restraint. The present context of this restraint also requires the creation of a more business-like environment for the efficient management of scarce resources.
I would like to affirm the government's continued commitment to occupational health and safety, and specifically to the work of the CCOHS. This has not changed. The centre has become renowned both internationally and throughout Canada as a dependable source of unbiased and highly professional information. There is no question that the vital task of delivering this information service relating to the health and safety of Canadians in their workplace will continue. I believe it will provide a better service in the future. It will provide a service that targets very real needs.
Mr. Speaker, recognizing your signal-it will provide an effective and efficient service in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to commend my colleague for Hamilton West for bringing forward this motion. It shows the insight and the initiative of this particular side of the House in understanding exactly
February 5, 1990

what the Canadian Centre for Occupational Elealth and Safety was really put in place to do.
Before we get into the nuts and bolts of the issue, I would like to read to members opposite, who seem to have swallowed the canary in believing everything the hon. member for Sarnia has said as it relates to this centre, because there is one particular problem here. When this centre was created by all-party support, that is, this side and that side and it just so happens we were on the other side at the time. When that took place there were certain individuals who spoke and one of them happened to be the hon. member for Vancouver South, who we all know very well as a respected member of the House. This is what he had to say: "As I understand it the only funds going into the centre come from the federal government". That will only change if there is agreement with the provinces.
The objectives of the centre-and I will read them for you-do not state, as members opposite have referred, that it is simply to send information out to those who request it for a fee. There is a little more to it than this.
The first and most important part of the mandate is to promote health and safety in the workplace and the physical and mental health of working people in Canada and through that, to facilitate consultation and co-operation among federal, provincial and territorial jurisdictions. Further, participation is necessary by labour and management in the establishment and maintenance of high standards of occupational health and safety appropriate to the Canadian situation.
If you take away that particular ability by removing funding from this centre, what you do is completely remove the mandate. That is, it is not possible to cany out the mandate. No member on the other side in this House has had the nerve to say that. Basically, what the CLC has said in their own way is that they cannot continue in their tripartite arrangement if the mandate changes. Once the funding is removed, then basically what has been done is remove the mandate and that is the enhancement of health and safety. It is easy enough to send out a fee. We could start up a company that could very easily do that for Canadians, that is to buy different discs of different issues and different health hazards all across the world and then sell them to people who are interested. That is not the intent of this centre. The

intent of this centre was to provide up-to-date unbiased information. It would go to whoever needed it. Access of information was based on the fact that you were Canadian, not that you had a dollar in your pocket to pay for it.
One of the reasons I thought it would be important for me to rise today is that I have taken the liberty of writing every premier and every minister of labour in the country to ask for their opinion of this, whether they thought it was a good idea to change the mandate of the Occupational Health and Safety Centre in Hamilton. I did this to find out if they agreed in essence with the government opposite and if it was nothing but opposition rhetoric that we have disagreed with the change in mandate.
I would just like to read a few into the record. From the letter from the Department of Labour of the great province of Prince Edward Island, I will read a few of the major paragraphs: "This decision will extremely prejudice the delivery of trustworthy and impartial information to individuals, unions, employers and governments which is so critically important in providing safe and healthy workplaces in the nation. The recent proclamation of the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System, a system that has been heralded throughout many nations of the world as progressive and far-sighted, is now being placed in jeopardy with this financial decision."
We go to the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador which is always willing to give us its advice on different issues. They state to us: "I have previously indicated my support for maintaining the status quo with respect to funding for the Canadian centre. The centre is an important national clearing house of occupational health and safety information and represents a major tangible effort to co-ordinate and harmonize occupational health and safety issues in Canada".
The important part is "harmonize and co-ordinate", not just grabbing information and shipping it out for a fee. That is not what we are talking about here. We are talking about enhancing and improving our workplace hazardous information, our safety in the workplace and that is a continuing process. That is not something that we can just turn off like a tap and say: "It is done. Now we will sell it to you." It continues day after day as new materials are invented and new processes are put in place. Therefore we have to continue to allow the centre

This centre is vital for the health and safety of firefighters involved in what has been traditionally called the most dangerous profession, but continues to be needed for the safety of all Canadians who are reliant on the information available on short notice".
Short notice is the important thing here. Do we wait until we send a bill, get the cheque and then send the information? Or do we, in essence, send the information when they need it at that moment? It would be interesting for the members opposite to understand this, the little fire departments do not have the dollars available. The mandate of this particular centre was simply that every single Canadian has the right to free access to health and safety information that relates to their workplace. We have now changed the mandate and I suggest very strongly that members opposite understand that before they vote against my friend's motion to change the approach and put funding back in place which was intended for this centre so we can continue our work as Canadians have done in the past and to be front and centre in the world and to try to make our workplaces safer and better places for us all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I entirely agree with my right hon. friend that the concept of bilingualism is a hallmark of the nation. Therefore I am assuming that we will have the support of the Prime Minister if our House leaders meet later this day to form such a motion. I do not dispute the Prime Minister's intentions.
In the same vein, I would also ask the Prime Minister if he has contacted provincial premiers and territorial leaders about this issue, which is becoming a continuing

February 5, 1990
Oral Questions
and very serious issue in Canada this week? We have to take some real leadership in this Chamber.
I would ask the Prime Minister: Has he contacted his colleagues in the provinces and the territories to discuss this issue? Has he called a meeting to discuss this issue, or will he agree to do so?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the question as to whether I have begun to speak to provincial premiers, the answer is yes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: On this issue?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Yes, on this issue.
My hon. friend expresses concern. This was a position, in terms of the hierarchy of concerns, that the previous Leader of the NDP expressed very eloquently and well on the floor of the House of Commons. He said time and time again and very persuasively that before some other important matters could be addressed we must repair the injustice of 1981-82 and bring Quebec back into the constitutional family.
The Meech Lake Accord, which deals with the fundamental issue of linguistic duality, English speaking minorities in the province of Quebec and French speaking minorities elsewhere, which spells it out very clearly, surely has to be part and parcel of any thought my hon. friend would give to any motion in promotion of bilingualism. So, clearly, if one came forward, I would count very much on her to express support for something which is so important to the province of Quebec and to Canada, namely, support for the Meech Lake Accord and all that it means to French speaking Canadians saying yes to Canada.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.

The Prime Minister must rise above all political partisanship. It is a question of national unity.
Why does he not support the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition for a unanimous motion of this House today?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, neither I nor the Leader of the Opposition made any partisan remark. He asked me a completely legitimate question and I gave him an answer which I hope was suitable. We will have discussions to see
whether some resolution could not be devised to promote the interests involved.
The Leader of the Opposition has always spoken and acted in favour of linguistic minorities, and so have I. The Leader of the Opposition has always acted and spoken in favour of the Meech Lake Accord because it will bring Quebec back into the Canadian Constitution. Talking about the problem of linguistic duality, which is mentioned in the Meech Lake Accord, and the problems of minorities, it seems to me that it is extremely difficult to present a resolution today that would ignore the problem of Quebec's exclusion, as in 1981. Nevertheless, it is a vital problem for Quebec, for Acadians, for francophones and for all of Canada.
So I agree with the Leader of the Opposition and perhaps with the Leader of the New Democratic Party that we should find a resolution honouring all our obligations for bilingualism nationally and for the Meech Lake Accord, which finally says yes to Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In the speech he gave in the House on the Organization of American States, the Prime Minister committed himself to a new role for Canada in the western hemisphere.
I have recently returned from a trip to El Salvador and, amongst the tragedy of that country, sensed a new desire to move a peace process forward. But it needs the help of other countries.

Oral Questions
pursuing human rights conditions, pursuing the democratic process and adding to the peace process, so that this country can give a very positive signal to the people of that region that we do care what happens to them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, given the interest of my hon. friend for the region, he will be pleased to know that yesterday I received a call from the President of Mexico, expressing gratitude to Canada for joining the OAS and, as well, for Canada's leadership on debt relief for Mexico, which he views as a very important instrument and which I think can be replicated in other countries of Latin America. I know my hon. friend would want to know that.
With regard to budgetary considerations, the Minister of Finance, at an appropriate time, will bring forth a budget which I hope will be able to satisfy the requirements and interests of my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister recognizes that conflict taking place in places like El Salvador. That is the key to peace in that entire region.
Is he prepared to use his good offices to make a representation to the Bush administration, which is presently looking at its own economic and military aid programs in Central America, and request that all U.S. aid, which is the major support of that country, be contingent upon recognition of human rights and upon the ability to bring the two sides to the table for a consecutive and ongoing negotiation toward a peace process? That kind of aid under that kind of condition would perhaps be the most important thing that could happen. Is the Prime Minister prepared to make that kind of representation to his colleague, the President of the United States?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we give a lot more aid on a per capita basis around the world than does the United States of America. Canada, on a per capita basis, is infinitely ahead of the United States of America, and we do not throw in military aid for the ends of the calculations either. I think the nation has an excellent record in terms of foreign

aid, without strings attached. That is what we propose to continue to do.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself have already spoken to the United States many times in regard to this approach for its foreign aid. The parliamentary committee discussed $100 million in aid to the region. It is our intention to make sure that undertaking is respected.
As the President of Mexico indicated yesterday, through the leadership of the Minister of Finance as chairman of the interim committee of the IMF with his role in Mexico, with the role of the Canadian chartered banks, plus the high per capita contribution of foreign aid, second only to France of the major industrialized nations of the world, Canada has provided a leadership role and will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture.
The farm debt crisis in Saskatchewan is continuing to deteriorate. Since 1985, 10,000 farmers have been served with foreclosure notices. The Farm Credit Corporation now owns some 475,000 acres in Saskatchewan.
Could the minister tell western farmers when he is going to bring in programs to keep farmers on the land rather than have their farms seized by the Farm Credit Corporation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just for the record, the hon. member might be interested in being reminded of the fact that when we came into office, as a result of the Liberal policies farm bankruptcies reached an all-time high of 551 in one year. That was in the year 1984. They have been reduced substantially, by at least 50 per cent. That is still too high.
The hon. member has been an ardent watcher of the agricultural policy review process that is being undertaken. I think that this government has truly acknowledged the fact that many of our safety nets and stabilization programs have been put through the supreme test over the course of the last five years because of drought, because of other natural disasters, and because of the low commodity prices. We are presently reviewing all these programs in an attempt to bring about a safety net, stabilization programs and improved crop insurance programs that will assist our farmers.
Oral Questions
In the meantime the farm debt review process is working very well. It has handled over 8,000 different applications and on 77 per cent of those occasions there have been satisfactory arrangements made.
All in all there is progress. We recognize the difficulty and the magnitude of the problem, but this government is working very closely with the farming community to try to bring about better policies to provide greater security and greater confidence for the future.

Mr. Speaker, I would just point out to the Minister of Agriculture that in 1985 there were some 500 bankruptcies in Saskatchewan. Last year there were 1,106.1 should point out that the impact of the farm crisis and farm debt spreads far beyond the farm to small communities. Some 23,000 left Saskatchewan last year.
On December 19, the Farm Credit Corporation in Saskatchewan sent out a notice to all real estate agents in north eastern Saskatchewan offering them a finder's fee of 5 per cent to buy up farmland and put farmers off the land.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows very well that under the farm debt review every attempt has been made to keep farmers on the land through short-term lease arrangements, through longer term lease arrangements, through consolidation, and through selling off some lands.
Every conceivable arrangement has been considered and the farm debt review board process has worked very well. This is where the creditors, the farmers, and the farm debt review board sit down together to try to work out the best available plan that can be arrived at. In some cases there is land that is put up for sale and there is land that is taken over by the Farm Credit Corporation.
We are attempting to sell off the land because it is not the intention of this government to hold on to large tracts of land. We are not in the business of owning land.

We are in the business of getting it back into the hands of the farmers, and that is what we intend to do.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the part-time Minister of Agriculture. The minister is aware that American subsidized wheat sales to traditional Canadian wheat markets are a devastating blow to the Canadian wheat farmer.

There is a price war going on. It is important to note the leadership of the Prime Minister by bringing agriculture to the top of the agenda at the Uruguay Round. We must resolve the problem of trade distorting subsidies that is hurting this country and hurting other medium sized exporters. We are in that process.
I can assure the hon. member and the farmers of Canada that, as we have demonstrated in the past, in the course of pursuing this we will certainly not stand idly by and see our farmers go down the drain.

Mr. Speaker, what the minister is saying is that there should be one set of trade laws for the Americans and a lesser set for Canadian farmers.
The minister should be aware that there is a real crisis in western Canada. Over 10,000 Saskatchewan farmers are expected to lose their farms this year. Farm income
in Saskatchewan is expected to drop 101 per cent, and 90 per cent in Manitoba.
Will the minister make a commitment in this House today to provide the operating capital necessary for Canadian grain farmers to plant their crops for this season so as to stop this agricultural devastation in our agricultural community?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council

Mr. Speaker, I said precisely the exact opposite. Again, if the member was not a part-time critic, he would know, as I have indicated in the House on many occasions, that we have at the present time a technical committee of assistant deputy ministers of the federal and provincial governments assessing the situation. I should remind him as well, in case he was not aware, that grain prices are about 50 per cent higher this year in the announced initial prices than they were in 1986. It is still too low, but there is some sign that prices are in fact strengthening.
We are examining the situation in terms of the impact of the lower commodity prices, the drought situation, the excessive moisture in some areas and the critical cash flow problems in others. The technical committee of federal and provincial ADMs is assessing this situation. We will have the interim preliminary data sometime later this month.
We hope at that particular time to assess the situation, to look at the application of the existing programs and, if there needs to be further assistance, the federal government and the provinces will come up with a package.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Due to the public outcry and the inflationary pressures of the 9 per cent GST, it has been reduced by 2 per cent. It has been reduced on everything except housing where it remains an effective 4.5 per cent, as originally planned. In light of the crisis of affordability of housing, particularly for young families and seniors, and the fact that many families are being driven into poverty by the high cost of housing, why did the minister not reduce the GST on housing by the 2 per cent?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. member would like to mislead the House. There is a reduction in the GST from 9 per cent to 7 per cent. There is a 2.5 per cent housing rebate. But there are also taxes today on a number of the things that are used to build a house, including building materials, plumbing supplies, rugs, windows and other material, all of which amount to about 4 per cent depending on the community.
When the hon. member says there is a 4.5 per cent tax, he is only telling half the story. The existing tax is around 4 per cent so that there is a small increase of the order of half of one per cent in his community. It may be somewhat lower or somewhat higher in others. I think we have treated the housing industry quite fairly, and we have certainly followed through on the commitment I gave in September 1988.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Minister of Finance.
There is a crisis in confidence about the government's statements that the GST will not affect affordable housing. The statements in its information pamphlet are pure garbage. The Canadian Home Builders Association and independent tax consultants say that the average price across Canada will increase $3,000; in Toronto $9,000. Housing consultants say that rents will increase by $300 and $400.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member put his question.
In light of these facts, how can the minister say that it will not drive up the cost of housing?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member is quite aware, rents are not taxed under the GST. Existing houses are not taxed under the GST. The impact of the 7 per cent tax, less the housing rebate, is about equivalent to the amount of tax that already applies to a house.
I suggest that indicates very clearly we have followed through on our commitment in September 1988 that what we would be doing with the GST would not adversely affect the affordability of housing.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certainly aware of the newspaper article. I am aware of the concerns of people that the existing manufacturers' sales tax will not be taken off many products, particularly with respect to building materials.
The hon. member and all members of the House should be aware that in the past there have actually been reductions in the federal sales tax on building materials and those have been reflected in the prices that have been charged to the public. In this case, with a very substantial reduction in the costs to the suppliers of building materials, that being the federal sales tax component, competition is obviously going to force that down just as it did in the past when there were reductions in the federal sales tax.
In addition to that, the Department of Finance will be putting in place a monitoring office to ensure that all consumers in Canada are quite aware of what prices should be once the manufacturers' sales tax, the federal sales tax, is removed. Also, that will operate as a complaint office once the new GST goes into effect and will be able to focus the spotlight of moral suasion on those people who persist in leaving the tax in place.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess there is nothing more precious about this place we call the Parliament of Canada than our capacity to speak in the Chamber, to listen to each other, to engage in vigorous debate on behalf of democracy and on behalf of good decisionmaking.
The last couple of weeks I have found particularly disturbing because of the extent to which tactics have been employed in the Chamber that bring the actions of the Chair into question but which, in the final analysis, are dedicated to reducing the possibility for us to engage in active debate.
I guess the best protection for us as a political party charged with the responsibility of governing this nation as we seek to do what is right but not necessarily popular, is that notion of free speech. Our protection lies in the facts and in the truth of the circumstances and the situation. It is what we predict will happen versus what the opposition predict will happen.
There are well over 100 members here today who were not here in 1984. That is when we announced our intention to examine the entire taxation system in this country and, in particular, the income tax system and the consumer taxation system.
We began a dialogue with Canadians back in 1984. We brought out a very extensive discussion paper close to three years ago. It was certainly available in my riding, and I would think in the ridings of all government members. We have made it available. Vigorously we went out into our communities and shared it with Chambers of Commerce, local business people and consumers groups. I am not sure that the members of the opposition did that. I am not sure that they want Canadians to know much about the current method of consumption taxation or about the possibility of proposed changes in relation to consumption taxation.
I am not sure they did because they knew that as we changed things for the better it would be hard for them to get the credit. They simply stood up and complained.
Government Orders
A complaint is nice, it is abrupt, it can be colourful. Complaints are easy. Explanation of complex events is difficult.
We went through what I consider to have been the bitterest election campaign in my experience in September, October, and November, 1988. What made it bitter was the fact that members of the opposition and their partisans went out to senior citizen complexes to tell Canadians: "If you pass the free trade deal, your pensions will be gone, your health care will be gone. All of the good things that you value about this country will be gone." That is what they went out and said one and a half years ago. Where did it get them? It got them another term in opposition.
Now they have started the same tactic a little bit earlier. Instead of starting it the last six months before an election, they are trying to start it three years ahead of time. What are they doing?
They are going out to the senior citizens' homes and telling the seniors that they are going to lose their medicare because the government is going to change the taxation system and that they are going to lose their pensions because the taxation system is going to be changed. Canadians have a memory. Canadians do have a bit of common sense. All of these half-truths and misunderstandings that members of the opposition are spreading are going to come back and bite them and choke them by the time the next federal election comes around. They are not true. They are telling Canadians things that are simply not true.
I heard somebody on CBC Newsworld the other day. That person had been listening to the opposition say: "Everything in Canada on January 1, 1991 will be 7 per cent more expensive. Get ready for it". I said who is there, other than a very busy person who does not take the time to think, who could make a statement like that about this change? Is there anybody with a modicum of common sense?
It is a bit like this. Let us say that we have to collect 10 cents of tax. Under the current system, let us say we tax glasses and we do not tax pens. Then we have to get 10 cents off the glasses, if we have to have 10 cents, and we are getting nothing off the pen. That is what the manufacturers' sales tax is about.
It takes half the things we buy in this country and puts a tax on them, a tax of 13.5 per cent. It collects $18,000

million that way, on half the things we buy in this country. The opposition comes along and says: "The dirty old government is going to put it on the glasses and the pen". We still have to collect 10 cents. If we are going to collect it on the glasses and the pen, we collect five cents on the pen and five cents on the glasses.

Then what happens? The pen is five cents more expensive, but the glasses are five cents cheaper.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Can the opposition understand that? Canadians can. If opposition members would pay a little bit of attention, they would know that we are going to put a tax on twice as many things and we are going to put it on at half as much. Thus half the things Canadians buy in the future will be cheaper and half the things they buy will be more expensive. That is the reality.
How can a 13.5 per cent tax be changed to a 7 per cent tax, a tax which is collected on twice as many things to gamer that amount of money, unless half the things we buy in this country are going to be cheaper in the future?
Is it just half? That is where the mathematics get a little more complex. I do not know who is coaching whom, whether it is the member for Calgary East or the Leader of the Official Opposition. Last week we had a lesson in mathematics from the two of them that was identical. Either that is a lucky break or one person on that side-the Leader of the Official Opposition-is coaching the member for Calgary East, or the member for Calgary East is coaching the Leader of the Official Opposition.
When I look around at the Conservative benches I am reminded that once upon a time I wanted to start a business. I had no customers, no machines, no employees, no warehouse, no nothing. It was to be an office coffee business. I went out and made sales and bought machines, employed people, met a payroll and I kept the books. I look at this tax and I say: "Gee, if I still had that business it would help me." I sold a product. I sold a thing. I sold coffee. The GST would help me. It would make the machines I bought cheaper. It would make the coffee pots I bought cheaper. It would make the soap I bought cheaper. All of the things that went into my business, the truck and the gasoline would be cheaper.
Therefore, I would have had to borrow less from the bank, pay less interest, and been in better shape.
I look around the Conservative benches and I see that there is somebody who owned a business, there is somebody, there is somebody, there is somebody, and there is somebody. I look over at the NDP and ask: "Is there anybody over there who ever owned a business?"
Yes.

budget. The Liberals and the NDP said it was an absolute catastrophe, it was going to cost this country hundreds of thousands of jobs and the unemployment roles would climb.
It is five years later. In every single province the unemployment rate is lower. There are 1.5 million more Canadians who have a job and pay tax than there were five years ago. These are the parties that stated: "You are going to lose your pensions. You are going to lose your health care if you continue free trade." There are almost 250,000 million more jobs in the first year of free trade. The jobs are better paid.
Did you see how much the average wages in this country climbed in the last 12 months, Mr. Speaker? It is an enormous increase. It runs to almost 9 per cent in some sectors. There are 750,000 people today who were on the poverty rolls when we came into office in 1984 who are not on the poverty rolls now. There are hundreds of thousands of children off the poverty rolls.
This is a government that has had a finance minister, instead of committees, instead of back-benchers, who has tried to consult with the Canadian people time after time to lay out the facts with the Canadian people time after time, and history says we are right.
Do all the senior citizens who are watching this program right now want me or my colleagues to explain in detail every little facet of the GST? Does that make sense? Do people need to know that? Do they need to understand it? I say, no, Mr. Speaker, but we are not afraid of that.
For the better part of a year we have had a hot line which has been advertised in newspapers. If anyone has a question about any little detail, he or she can phone that number free of charge. We are not afraid of the facts. We are not afraid of the details. How many members on the opposite side are telling their constituents to phone the number and get the facts? Or do they say: "Listen to me and my biased householders and my misinformation campaign?" Which is it? Phone the number and get the facts or listen to me and the nonsense I am sending out there?

I say to those senior citizens that they can listen to one party in this Chamber, just one, if they want to understand the future and the truth about the future. That is the party that has been right for six years in a row now.

I do not know what it will take to convince members of the opposition that attempting to fool the Canadian people is a mug's game, a loser's game. Those of you in the Liberal party who were not here back in 1980 to 1984, for example, when your party was in power and finance minister after finance minister went public with an incorrect picture of the state of the economy. In 1984 it was the biggest defeat in the history of your party because consistently your finance minister and your back-benchers went forward with a picture based not on fact but on fiction. Canadians are a people with their feet on the ground, with an awful lot of common sense, and they can tell fact from fiction.
You have won a short-term victory, because you have had a lot of help. You have chambers of commerce that are out fighting on behalf of their members, you have had the Federation of Independent Business, you have had the "Axe the Tax", and many groups that have stated that they will fight this tax on your behalf, including your own parties, and "send me a donation". That is what all those groups have in common. "I will fight, but send me a donation that I can use to fight".
It is not a perfect tax. No one on this side believes that there is any such thing as a perfect tax. But we have an obligation as members of this House to determine whether it is a better tax, whether it is a better system of taxation.

Mr. Speaker, if you cut through all the nonsense, they want to say to Canadians that a 13.5 percent tax is better than a 7 per cent tax. That is a hard sell. Canadians, they want you to believe that a 13.5 per cent tax is better than 7 per cent. They want you to believe, Mr. Speaker, that taxing a domestic business heavier than an import business is good for jobs. Raising the price on things we make in Canada while at the same time not raising the price on things we import is somehow going to produce better jobs and more jobs for Canadians. That is what they want you to believe, Canadians. I think that is a hard sell. In 1924 we were the first country in the world to bring in the tax. A lot of countries copied us. Every single one of them has got rid of that tax. In 65 years people copied us coming in. They found out the problem with it and stopped.
Popularity is not what governing is about. It is doing what is right, what is sensible. Using common sense on behalf of Canadian people is what governing is all about. They will and they have convinced the Canadian people in the short term that there is something wrong. Over the long term Canadians will discover there is something right about what we are doing, that it is logical, that it makes sense, that it is good for the economy and good for the social welfare system. When they find that out, they will not forget who was lying to them and those who lied to them will get their just desserts the same way they did in November 1988.

I have two questions for the hon. member who spent some time leaving the impression that he was speaking the undying truth and everyone on this side of the Chamber was lying. There are two items that I want to raise with the member. I note that in his party's outlook in 1984-85 when the Minister of Finance first began his taxation and expenditure program, he made the statement that if we continued to pursue the Liberal line of spending and taxation that within five years the deficit would have doubled. In fact, we have instead pursued a Conservative line of expenditures and taxation and the deficit has more than doubled.
Would he tell us what went wrong. Why did they point their fingers at the Liberals and then pursue an even
more onerous proposition? Perhaps he could explain that, since he is in a truth-telling mood.
Also, while he is in a truth-telling mood, would he please try to explain to the people of Canada, since the people in the House know what the answer is, why he attempted to mislead the people of Canada with his statements over the weekend about the cost of maintaining the House of Commons. He left the impression that when the House was sitting it costs $1 million a day and leaves the obviously wrong conclusion that if the House was not sitting the cost would be zero. I have looked back at a few of the records. I remember noting a year ago that the House did not sit for the month of February. It sat for the whole of the month of February the year before. The costs for the year we did not sit were actually considerably higher than when we were sitting.
I submit that the hon. Whip of the government side knows that the cost of the House of Commons goes on and varies barely a tiddle or a jot whether we sit or we do not sit. It is a fixed cost and not much can be done about it. The restaurants may cost a little less when we are not sitting, but there is no business coming through to offset their costs either. In fact, the practice and the facts are that when we do not sit, it has been costing us more than when we do sit. Why did he try to leave the false impression that somehow by tying up time in the House we are costing $1 million a day when he knows better?

The Leader of the Official Opposition with a minority government took Canada from a position of basically a balanced budget, where we were not using any money for payment on interest, and into big debts.
They used that minority government period to create the big debt that grew and grew. When we came into office the government of the day, supported in large part by the New Democratic Party, was borrowing $16,000 million for programs, plus another $22 million for interest payments.
Well, it is five years later and we have a surplus. We have changed. We have cut to the point where on programs we do not borrow a dime. On a net basis over five years, we have not. We, in fact have $9 billion that goes to pay the interest on the public debt. The interest payment this year is over $38 billion, the deficit is only $30 billion. Where does the money come from if it does not come from a surplus on programs? Members opposite may not quite comprehend all of that because there is a lot of technical vocabulary in that, a difference between the words debt and deficit and surplus, and so on.
We have created 1.5 million jobs with our economic program. If we had listened to the Leader of the NDP, he was predicting a job loss of 184,000, let us say a couple of hundred thousand each year. That would be a million more unemployed, instead of 1.5 million working. That is a 2.5 million turn around. That is 10 per cent of the Canadian population, the difference between their prediction and our prediction and what it would do. That is why so many people are off the poverty rolls. That is why so many more people have a job. That is why the average wage is up so much. That is why the standard of living is up so much. That is why the productivity of the Canadian economy is up so much. To the Canadian people, I say: "follow our advice".

Why has the Minister of Finance not listened to Canadians? Why has the Department of Finance not listened to Canadians? Why has the Conservative government not listened to Canadians?
The government's track record is one of not listening. It's track record really speaks for itself because it does not see this to be a problem. It has stated right along that the Liberals left a legacy of high debt, of high interest payments. We should look very carefully at the government's record and try to examine what, in fact, really did happen. When this government took power in 1984, the debt was approximately $170 billion. Today, the debt is $350 billion. It has doubled the debt in five short years.
What about taxes? What about the gross income of this country, federally, in taxes? When the government took power in 1984, taxes through the federal government sources were $70 billion. Today, the taxes bring in $120 billion. It has increased taxes by $50 billion in this country, over 70 per cent.
Canadians are upset because in five years our taxes have gone up over 70 per cent. The debt has been doubled. The government talks about the debt charges. When the government took office, the debt charges were $22 billion. Today, they are $40 billion. It doubled the cost of paying those charges as well.
The government's track record, financially, is a fiasco. It doubled what Canada owes. It doubled the cost of paying that debt and it increased taxes over 70 per cent. Those are the simple facts that it does not talk about.
The government talks about how it has dealt with the deficit. The average Canadian knows that it has not really changed the deficit significantly. Thirty billion dollars a year every year for five years is its record. That is not doing a good job.
Let us look at what the chamber of commerce said in the pre-budget report to the government, to the Minister of Finance and to the Department of Finance. The chamber of commerce stated very clearly that it expected the government in 1984 to follow a careful plan in order to deal with debt, but that the government had shown no leadership in its five years in office. This is a strong indictment of what the government has done.

We must remember that this government has been in power during times when interest rates have been low, the lowest in the decade. The benefit of a growing economy has been there and good times for Canada have been there, but the government showed no leadership in dealing with the finances of this country.
The government has introduced 31 tax increases in Canada in its five years. This leads us to tax increase number 32, the GST. That seems to me a pretty poor direction in which to be heading.
Canadians are upset with being told they are doing well when the reality is that our debt is growing and the only method used to deal with the problem is to increase taxes again. We have to look at where we are going.
According to the government's statements over the past year, one finds that the government has said that taxes should be simple, at least simpler than existing taxes if we are to have good reform. The Minister of Finance said that the tax must be fair to all Canadians, visible, integrated with the provincial taxes which exist and revenue neutral.

He would have closed loopholes and lowered interest rates. He would have dealt with the debt and the deficit in other ways that would have been more reasonable.
We listen to Canadians across this country who are quite upset about what is going on in the country. The Progressive Conservatives were the authors of the free trade agreement. They authored 31 tax hikes. They authored the GST and they have authored pessimistic

I have not seen him dancing with joy over VIA or the armed forces bases, over taxing back pension, family allowances and so on. At the same time he is criticizing all of the tax increases.
The question I want to ask is simple. Recognizing that we have a debt problem, at the same time criticizing every attempt to reduce spending and at the same time criticizing every tax increase, how would the hon. mem-
February 5, 1990

ber propose to deal with the debt and the deficit problem?

Mr. Speaker, I am going to give a short answer.
