speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur has the floor for 10 minutes, plus 5 minutes for questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, the new goods and services tax unveiled by the federal government will be the most substantial tax levied on Canadians since the beginning of our history.
Actually, this tax has has nothing positive to offer. It is complex, regressive, inflationary and a prospective administrative nightmare for companies and businesses across the country.
The Conservative GST will hit many essential services purchased by average citizens. In fact, only basic groceries, prescription drugs and medical devices will be fully exempted. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) also told us that a number of essential services would also be exempted, which does not mean they will not be affected by the new tax.
For instance, a so-called exempt day care centre will not charge parents the GST directly. However, it will
Government Orders
have to pay the GST on all purchases of books, equipment and so forth. It will therefore have to charge more for its services to compensate for the extra cost. As you see, in spite of the so-called exemption, the GST will affect the price of day care services, and the consumer ends up footing the bill.
The burden on Canadians will be endless. From now on, taxable items will include haircuts, funerals, vending machine sales, shoes, restaurant meals but not food products purchased in grocery stores, car repairs, plane tickets, clothes, stamps and items that average citizens purchase every day.
Mr. Speaker, there is one rather interesting item in all this mess. During the last election campaign, the Minister of Finance promised all Canadians across the country that he would not introduce a goods and services tax without the co-operation of the provinces. In fact, he solemnly swore across this country, during that same campaign, that if he did introduce a goods and services tax, it would not increase the government's revenue. He swore that if he introduced a GST, it would not be inflationary and that it would be visible.
Empty promises! He reneged on practically all his promises about the GST.
We can certainly not accuse the Minister of Finance of being consistent.
This was the minister who said that the manufacturers' sales tax was quietly killing jobs. Nevertheless, he increased that same tax four times, raising it from 9 per cent to 10, 11, 12 and finally 13.5 per cent.
In 1984, the Minister of Finance promised Canadians that he would not increase taxes a single cent. Since he and his government took power, they raised them 31 times. It is absolutely incredible.
Although this tax will go from 9 to 7 per cent, the principle remains the same. It is completely contrary to the basic equity of a progressive tax system that takes money from people based on their income.
This tax hits everyone on all purchases and all services. It is not a discretionary tax. No one can go without buying food. People have to buy clothes for their children. Many services are absolutely essential, whether for

February 5, 1990
Government Orders
a pensioner or a family trying to make ends meet. They still have to buy things, so the principle remains.
It is the principle of taking the most from those who have the least, because they are the ones in society who are least able to be heard. They struggle every day to earn their living: workers on low and moderate incomes.
The fraudulent part of all this is that the minister hopes the headlines will say that he has reduced the tax from 9 to 7 per cent. In reality, all the revenue he gave up by doing so has been made up for by other taxes. In other words, the minister is pulling the wool over people's eyes. There is no tax reduction. I want to tell you that. He has simply transferred the burden to the middle class, the disadvantaged regions, pensioners and families receiving allowances.
When the minister announced that the GST would go from 9 to 7 per cent, he admitted that he had lost all control over the economy and the deficit, despite what he says. This is a minister who has doubled the public debt, that is, the total debt which this country has accumulated since Confederation, in only five years. It went from $170 billion to $350 billion in spite of all the tax increases in the last four or five years. In constant dollars, Canadian families are paying 30 per cent more in taxes than when the minister took office.
Obviously, the minister and his government are not to be trusted. They tell us that the GST will be 7 per cent, but what guarantee do we have that the Minister of Finance will not raise it? In fact, he recently refused to make a formal commitment not to raise the rate from 7 per cent in the future. Since the tax is invisible, the government can increase it more easily, which is what has happened abroad.

From the beginning the Minister of Finance has withheld the truth concerning the GST from Canadians. That minister has no more credibility. That minister has lost the confidence of Canadians from Vancouver to St. John's. Virtually every promise the minister has made concerning the GST has been broken.
For example, he promised that it would be revenue neutral. Is it revenue neutral? No, it is not. He promised that it would be visible. Is it visible? It may be. It may not be. We are not sure. He promised that it would be
simple. It certainly is not. The Minister of Finance promised that small businesses would be adequately compensated for implementing the GST and that this tax would be fair to middle and low income Canadians. More broken promises, Mr. Speaker.
Finally, he promised to remove surtaxes on personal income as part of tax reform. Instead he has made them permanent. As an Atlantic Canadian I am particularly distressed that the GST will shift the tax burden from central Canada to other regions. The evidence presented to the finance committee clearly confirms that the GST will penalize regions for being located far away from the large consumer markets and manufacturing centres in central Canada.
Despite strong evidence that the GST will create greater regional disparities within Canada, there is no indication from either the government or the Conservative members of the finance committee that they either understand this shift or care about it.
In conclusion, I would like to say that the government's attempt at imposing this tax on the people of Canada proves one thing beyond all doubt. It proves that the government has lost control of the economy. Despite all the rhetoric concerning the deficit and the debt, this government has lost control of our country's finances. The finance minister has doubled the total public debt of this country, which is to say the cumulative debt since Confederation. He has doubled it in five years from $170 billion to $350 billion despite the greatest tax increases witnessed in Canadian history. He has imposed up to 31 tax increases. Canadians have had enough.
The Conservative goods and services tax proposal is seriously flawed and must be scrapped. Moreover, the federal government must immediately begin consultations with Canadians and provincial governments on the creation of a fair and integrated reform of the entire tax system. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, to all members in the House and to the Canadian public that it is time to go back to the drawing board. Let's scrap this tax.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested to hear some of the member's comments about the effect of the proposed goods and services tax. Many of those are comments that I have heard from my own constituents. Around 30,000 people left the province of Saskatchewan

last year because of the lack of business opportunities and the lack of cash income on farms, the international trade situation being what it is.
The business community there says that the high interest rates have become chronic and represent a financial grab by central Canada with the money draining out of the business community of that region into central Canada. In addition, they see this tax as being not only a pain in the neck that they do not need at a time when business is very tough, but as another decrease in the amount of money available in the small towns and remote regions of this community.
Is that the way the hon. member sees this tax as well?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his comments. I think he summarized it quite well. The government's interest rate policy is in place to help alleviate the situation in central Canada, especially southern Ontario where they have a very hot, inflationist economy. I think the outer regions-western Canada, eastern Canada and the north-are suffering because of that.
It is about time the government has a look at those types of policies along with this tax, because I am told that if the interest rate is lowered by one point the government would save $1.6 billion. The government talks about saving. It cuts VIA Rail because it wanted to save $500 million. Why can the government not cut the interest rate? It says it is not that simple. I say that we should look at that a little more. If we do that along with a number of other new economic policies, I think we can do it.
As far as the tax itself, it is certainly going to cause some major problems. We talk about it being very regressive. It is certainly a regressive tax. Possibly it will also cause a state of recession. Certainly that is going to be a major problem for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to Bill C-62.1 am in favour of the principle of sales tax reform in Canada. I emphasize the word "reform" because there are those who for selfish and partisan reasons persist in calling the GST a new tax. In so doing they imply that there is no present federal sales tax.
The fact is that Canada has had a sales tax, federally, since 1924. It is hidden deep in the price of all goods and services in Canada.
First, the federal sales taxes apply at rates of 9 per cent, 11 per cent, 13.5 per cent or as much as 19 per cent on sales of certain goods from the manufacturer. On top of that, there is a significant additional amount of federal sales tax paid on things that are used in the production of all other goods and services. These are input costs like vehicles, fuel, computers, telephone services, office furniture and equipment, stationery, construction materials and many more.
This additional amount results from cascading, tax on tax on tax, in each step between the raw material and the finished product. At present there is an additional tax burden of between 1 and 3 per cent on the selling price of an item as a result of cascading. There are those who may say, "So what?" Some of them are across the aisle. We have had the tax for 66 years. We survived. Why change it? Why reform sales tax at all?
First, the taxation of the inputs used to produce domestic goods harms Canada's international competitiveness. The goods we want to export bear the hidden burden of the current federal manufacturers' sales tax.
February 5, 1990

Second, the existing federal sales tax favours imported goods over domestically produced goods. Our domestically manufactured products are taxed on an average one third higher than competing imports. This is because the inputs are taxed on their value upon entry into Canada before a number of inputs such as further processing, advertising, distribution, marketing, packaging and other costs are added on to the value of that product. Whereas, the competing Canadian product is taxed further on in the chain after a number of these additional inputs have been factored in.
In an increasingly interdependent world, competition is such that we in Canada can no longer see our manufacturing sector trying to gain a share of the world market with one hand tied behind its back. Our enhanced ability to compete in the world will mean more jobs in Canadian manufacturing and industry. Adherence to the existing federal sales tax means more imports and fewer jobs at home.
Third, the existing federal sales tax is a jungle of regulation, special provisions, rulings, and administrative interpretations that generally evolve around the question: At which stage in the chain of value-added should the tax be imposed? Obviously, the earlier in the process the tax is applied, the lower the amount of tax-

Just as an aside, it is interesting that those who a few moments ago were professing interest in debating the merits of the GST are now trying by procedural measures to delay things even further.
Out of 75,000 manufacturers, there have been 23,000 separate legal rulings, and you can hardly blame manufacturers for trying to minimize the GST as they attempt to compete against foreign importers.

The Auditor General recently pointed out that the use of marketing companies costs an estimated $350 million a year in sales tax leakage. Other avoidance and evasion measures may add up to as much as $2 billion a year. Clearly, the federal government has to eliminate the incentive to resort to complex avoidance mechanisms. The answer is to reform sales tax entirely, to totally remove it from production as all other nations in the world have done. We remain the only country in the world which taxes its own production inputs thereby pricing our products out of the world market and enhancing the opportunity for foreign competition while at the same time encouraging elaborate tax avoidance and evasion techniques at home.
These are the reasons why most informed Canadians and, indeed, all political parties have recognized that the existing federal manufacturers' sales tax must go. It is fundamentally flawed. It is capricious in its application and damaging to our economy. This is why the finance committee of this House, composed of members from all sides, recommended that Canada implement a multistage sales tax on the broadest possible base.
The existing federal sales tax raises some $18 billion in federal revenue. A replacement tax clearly must raise an equivalent amount. A perfect GST system would tax all goods and services in the country. This would provide the broadest base to which the lowest percentage rate could be applied in order to produce that amount of revenue. But most Canadians feel that certain goods and services should be exempted. That is certainly the position of this government and the opposition parties. That is why basic groceries and prescription drugs, medical devices, residential rents, the purchase of existing homes and a number of other health and education related items are tax free.
The various exemptions narrow the base. That means that the percentage rate of tax has to be higher than would be the case if the base were broader.

Mr. Speaker, the GST, from the viewpoint of the consumer, is similar to retail taxes operated by nine of the provinces in Canada at the present time.
The major difference between the GST and retail sales tax is that the GST will be collected at each stage of the production and distribution chain with businesses claiming full credits for all tax paid on their business purchases. Only in this way, through the collection and rebate at each stage, can all of the GST be eliminated on business inputs thereby removing the hidden cost of the current federal manufacturers' sales tax for both businesses and consumers.
The replacement of the existing federal sales tax with the GST will enable our productive sector to better compete in the world marketplace. The GST is designed, as I understand it, to be revenue neutral. To the extent that it succeeds in plugging the kind of leakage that the Auditor General has pointed out-which some estimate as much as $2 billion a year-to the extent that at least a part of the underground economy will be forced above ground because the multi-state sales tax is much harder to avoid than a tax paid only at the point of sale, to the extent that more people will likely be employed in the manufacturing and business sector thereby contributing to the tax system rather than taking from it, there will hopefully be additional revenues generated. These revenues will contribute to deficit and debt reduction thereby ensuring that the essential programs and services, which constitute the Canadian social safety net and which Canadians value, can continue to be met.
By continuing to generate a portion of over-all government revenues from consumption, which is a tax on spending, as opposed to income taxation which is a tax on
productivity the over-all fairness of the system will be maintained.
I personally believe that we cannot rely entirely on income taxation to generate revenues within Canada. There is a point, in my mind personally, at 50 per cent beyond which you are penalizing income which could be used for investment purposes. To the extent that people have moneys left over after the basics and after income tax they can spend it at their discretion as they choose or they can save it and invest. If they spend the money they will pay the GST-a consumption tax on what they spend. On the other hand, if they invest the moneys it will mean new capital, new plant, equipment, inventory, and jobs for Canadians.
There will be a refundable GST credit introduced to protect lower and modest income Canadians to the point where families with incomes of up to $30,000 a year will pay less tax than they do now.
The area that I represent is almost entirely dependent on agriculture and particularly the health of the export grain sector. That sector, at the moment, is terribly depressed as a result of the on-going trade subsidy war between the United States and the European community. I would therefore like to speak about the GST from the perspective of agriculture, and in doing so I would confess that I am sick, tired and weary of hearing special interest groups distorting the GST, and spreading untruths about it.
To hear the Canadian Federation of Independent Business quoted as saying to the farmer: "The implications for agriculture are staggering. You will soon be paying an extra 7 per cent retail tax on fertilizer, chemical fuels, equipment, et cetera." That statement is false. It is 100 per cent wrong. The fact is that the GST does not apply to production inputs of any kind whether they be agricultural, small business, manufacturing or industry. It does not apply to the purchase of goods and services that are used in a production chain, plain and simply. Under the current federal sales tax system many goods used in farming are tax exempt.
Like what?

However, other things that a farmer uses in the course of his farming operations are taxed, generally at a rate of 13.5 per cent on the manufacturing cost. These items include half-ton trucks, tools, some repair parts, construction materials for farm-building fences, fuel for
February 5, 1990

on highway use, and office equipment like computers. A half-ton truck for farm use, for example, which presently retails at approximately $14,000 should be some $1,400 less than would otherwise be the case as a result of the elimination of the existing federal manufacturers' sales tax and the rebate of GST to a farm purchaser.
Indeed a passenger vehicle of similar value purchased by a city dweller should be roughly $600 less owing to the difference between the current tax and the proposed GST. The naysayers and the doubting Thomases raise the question, "Will this saving be passed on?" I have no doubt that it will because we have in this country a competitive market-place, one that is based upon supply and demand. We have some 800,000 small businesses in this country, the backbone of the country, which compete with each other, which deal in large volume and small markup. I have no doubt that they will pass on the elimination of the FMST as well as the elimination of the cascading effect of that harmful tax to their customers. To believe otherwise would suggest that there are
800,000	small businesses in this country which collude and agree with each other every day to raise prices in concert. I think that is utter nonsense.
It is interesting to compare our system which is market driven, driven by supply and demand, with that kind of centrally planned economy which you have in eastern Europe and other nations in the world and which is being shown, day by day, to have failed utterly.
Even goods that are specifically exempt under the current sales tax regime contain a significant element of hidden tax, that is between 1 per cent and 3 per cent included in their price. This results from the cascading effect of the existing manufacturers' sales tax paid on many of the input costs that manufacturers and distributors have to buy in order to run their businesses.
Agricultural producers will note with satisfaction that the GST has been designed so that all producers, including farmers, get back all the sales tax they pay on their business inputs. The result will be real savings in operating costs. Under tax reform businesses pay a GST on the goods and services they buy and charge GST on their sales. The difference is remitted to the government. If the business in a particular period of time pays
Government Orders
out more tax than it collects the government will refund the difference.
Most all sales by farmers are zero rated so they will not charge any tax in their sales but they will still, of course, be able to claim refunds for all GST paid on their business input purchases. Producers will receive a refund within 21 days or the government will pay interest on the money. In many cases it should be possible to get the rebate before the account is paid.
Some may say why can we not be exempted altogether with some kind of an exemption certificate. The problem is that the more exemptions you have the more complex the system becomes. It would be difficult for vendors to differentiate between exempt and non-exempt customers. It would make administration more difficult so, in most instances, the producer like anyone else will pay the GST in his purchases. He can then apply for a refund of the GST paid on all of the business input purchases. In order to avoid temporarily tying up large amounts of money there is now being prepared a list of selected major items which will be unconditionally tax free. This list of items used exclusively by farmers is being developed in consultation with representatives of the farm community. The list will include combines and other big-ticket items not bought by people other than producers.
Transfers of land within the family will be tax free. So too will dispositions of land as part of the sale of the farm as a going concern. Other sales will be subject to tax because of the difficulty in determining the ultimate use. If the purchase is for farming or other business usage the purchaser will be able to claim a refund of the GST paid. Crop share paid as part of a rental agreement will be exempt from the GST. Cash rental payments and custom work will be taxable, again to assist in the administration of the tax. In situations where it is difficult to ascertain the purpose, such as custom snow removal, the tax is paid by the purchaser who, if eligible, can then claim the refund.
In regard to fuel, gasoline and diesel, the farmer presently receives a rebate of the federal sales tax and purchases for off highway production purposes. Under the GST, farmers will recover all GST paid on fuel purchases for the farming operation and, unlike the current system, the rebate will apply to fuel used both on highway and off highway as long as it is used for business purposes. Invoices will show the GST as a separate item or as included in the price. In either case, farmers will

February 5, 1990
Government Orders
have the same number of invoices as they have now and it will be a fairly straightforward matter to calculate the GST actually paid on business input which will be refundable. The bottom line is that farmers, like all other businesses, will be better treated under the GST than they now are under the federal manufacturers' sales tax.
The bottom line for the nation is a level playing field for Canadian producers, an economy in which imports will not be favoured but rather will be taxed in the same manner as Canadian-made goods. It will be an economy in which a hidden federal sales tax will be removed from the production of goods and services in Canada and from Canada's exports, thereby enabling Canadians to compete better, to expand sales, and to employ more Canadians.
Much of the criticism of the GST is tied into the perception that this is a new tax rather than a replacement tax. Coupled with the opposition to the GST is the common statement that the federal government, indeed governments at all levels, must demonstrate restraint, stop needless spending and eliminate waste and so on. We certainly subscribe to that. Indeed, we would invite an examination of a long list of program cuts and expenditure reductions, all of which have been criticized by those opposite.
This leads me to consideration of the current federal debt situation. We have moved in five short years from a $16 billion shortfall on federal current programs under the previous administration to a $9 billion surplus today. This clearly is still not good enough and much more has to be done.
The annual deficit must first be reduced, then eliminated, and ultimately we must begin making payments on the principal itself. The national debt imposes on the government of today the obligation to repay the overspending of the past. This debt will not go away. We cannot wish it away and we cannot ignore it. Indeed, if serious measures are not taken to deal with this problem now we shall soon reach the point where interest payments will consume so much of government revenue that there will not be enough left to maintain the most basic program needs of Canadians. There is no easy
answer. The choices are difficult. We can act responsibly through a combination of spending reductions and revenue increases designed to reduce and eventually eliminate the annual deficit, or we can go the other way. We can pretend the problem does not exist and go the South American way. We can simply print money and attempt to service the debt with cheap dollars. The result of this irresponsible action would be hyper-inflation, incredibly high interest rates, and massive unemployment.
There is still time to take control of the debt-deficit problem. To do so will test the resolve and determination of all Canadians. We have put in place over the past five years a number of policies designed to improve Canada's competitive position in the world because this means jobs for Canadians and a better future. Part and parcel of this initiative is sales tax reform.
In conclusion, I want to say that it is time to act. We have been talking about sales tax reform for 50 years. That is long enough. We have the GST proposal before this House. No one has been able to find any useful or viable alternative. No one has any other suggestions. We know that the federal manufacturers' sales tax has to go. Everyone knows it. All parties agree. The GST may not be perfect. Indeed, it is far from perfect. But it appears to be the only alternative and it is light years better than what we have now. I say let us get on with it for the sake of the country.

Mr. Speaker, to my honourable colleague, I have difficulty putting together two points that he raised in his speech. He raised the point that this tax is going to be revenue neutral and then in conclusion he states that this tax will, in fact, help pay off the programs initiated and a lot of other things.
In light of comments made by the Chamber of Commerce to this government suggesting that increases to spending by this government have been $50 billion over the last five years and 31 increases, how does he claim accountability with that question before him?

Mr. Speaker, unlike the hon. member I will attempt to answer the question put to me. I think there were two questions folded into the comment and question. One, if I recall it correctly, related to the question of neutrality. The other one related to accountability.
February 5, 1990

In regard to neutrality, it is my understanding that the tax has been designed to replace the revenue which the existing federal manufacturers' sales tax currently generates. It is also my understanding that the Auditor General has pointed out that there is leakage as a result of marketing companies of some $350 million a year.
There are others in the country who point out other loopholes, other inequities, other unfairnesses, other avoidance and evasion mechanisms which may add up to as much as $2 billion a year. There is an underground economy out there which will be more difficult to operate in as a result of the multi-stage nature of the tax.
Clearly, there is the potential for revenue which ought to be collected at this point in time to be collected. To the extent that that happens, this tax will have been a success. I believe it could generate more revenue.
There is a second aspect to it. This involves the projections of increased employment in Canada's manufacturing and industrial sector. It is pretty clear that if our productive sector is relieved of production input taxes, both direct and through the cascading effect of the existing federal manufacturers' sales tax, then it should put that sector in a better competitive position. It should result in more sales, in more exports, and in more employment in this country. There will be a lot of people paying into this system rather than taking out of it.
That has characterized the policy of this administration. It is policies like this which have resulted in something in the order of 1,600,000 more Canadians working today than was the case just five short years ago under the previous administration, an administration which spent this country into catastrophic debt and which mortgaged the future of Canadians.
You doubled it.

We doubled it, the hon. member says. The fact is that the debt which was inherited on March 31, 1985, at the end of the previous administration, was $199 billion. Members opposite do not want to hear the truth. The fact is that the effect of compound interest on that $199 billion accounts for every cent of the increase in the
Government Orders
national debt from March 31, 1985 to March 31, 1990. Every cent of the increase in the national debt is simply unpaid compound interest on the profligate over-spending of the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to hear my colleague so succinctly detail the benefits of the GST. Coming from a region of this nation which has for years been export oriented but which has suffered under the old system of the FST, we will now benefit from the imposition of the GST which will induce exporters in our region to be more competitive in the future. Hopefully, it will have the effect of bringing even more businesses into Atlantic Canada, as has been the trend over the past five years.
I also want to say that I am pleased to hear why consumers and all Canadians should not be skeptical that manufacturers will pass on the savings of the FST to them because of what has already been outlined.
I would just like to briefly comment that we often hear opposition members say that 70 per cent of the people are against the GST. In my experience, 70 per cent or more of the people would respond that they were negative to taxes anyway, regardless of what that tax might be and who imposes it.
My question to my hon. colleague is this. In his experience, what would be the response in his constituency to the question: "Are you in favour of government services"?

Mr. Speaker, there is clearly a problem. Canadians want continued services. They have been accustomed to a myriad of services from the federal government, and there is nothing wrong with that.
What is wrong is that previous administrations never had the courage to tax Canadians sufficiently to pay for those services and for those programs. There is a movement called Resolution One. I believe that Resolution One in the British North America Act ought to have been the clause stating that senior levels of government

February 5, 1990

had to balance their books on an annual basis except in a time of dire emergency, such as war.
Had that been the case the spendthrift group under Prime Minister Trudeau would not have been in a position to mortgage this country to the hilt and put us in the position today where we are scrambling to pay off the debt of the past rather than being in a position to build and invest for the future. Mr. Speaker, I have a few short questions. First, the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia said that no one has made any suggestions other than the GST. I remember in the finance committee I heard a lot of alternatives, a lot of suggestions. Some were good and some were probably not so good.

Second, when in a democratic system is it incumbent upon him as a member of Parliament representing his own riding, his own constituents, to stand up and say: "No"? The Gallup poll last week showed that 74 per cent of the people are opposed to the GST. The poll today shows 79 per cent.
It is not good enough that the member for New Brunswick said that people are against taxes. We find today in The Globe and Mail, for example, that 56 per cent of the people who smoke cigarettes would favour an increase of 50 cents a pack in the tax on cigarettes. There are certain taxes in this country that are supported by the people. I do not think it is good enough just to say that people do not want tax increases.
How can he say that no one has made any other suggestions? At what point must a member of Parliament get up in this House and support his or her constituents, in this case 79 per cent of the people in this country who are against the GST? An overwhelming number of Conservative voters from 1988 are in opposition to the GST. Is it not incumbent upon that member to get up in this House and represent their point of view?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question raised by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville.
First, he asked if there were alternatives put in regard to the GST, or for sales tax reform. No doubt he is referring to those put forward by his own party in a minority report attached to the finance committee's deliberations on the sales tax reform question.
In my remarks earlier I talked in terms of viable, practical, sensible solutions and alternatives. Of course, in saying that I thought the hon. member would understand that it automatically excluded the addendum to the finance report put forward by the NDP.
Since he has raised the matter I will give members of the NDP a compliment. I will say that at least they have put forward some alternatives. They did that, unlike the Liberals whose only answer is to criticize, criticize, criticize endlessly and mindlessly. The NDP did put forward some suggestions, and indeed I looked at them.
They were in terms of hiking the marginal tax rate. I talked about that in my speech. We do not need a 67 per cent income tax rate in this country. You have got to give people a little bit of room to be productive and to have some incentive to grow. Personally, I reject that. I suggest to the hon. member that most Canadians would.
Another thing members of the NDP talked about was to bring back the estate tax. I thought they learned their lesson in Saskatchewan back in the 1970s. But they want to bring back the estate tax to "get the wealthy", the same "wealthy" that they are protecting every day in this House by objecting to taxing back old age pension and family allowance from higher income Canadians-a totally inconsistent policy and one which makes no sense.
The second point the hon. member suggests is that we should abolish Parliament, I guess, and just let the bureaucrats run the country based on a Gallup poll that comes out every Friday. Maybe that is the answer. I do not know.
The fact is that if we govern by polls in this country I do not know where we would be. I am not particularly interested in polls, whether they are Gallup polls or
February 5, 1990

whether they are the polls which the NDP pays people in the United States to do.
The only poll which has the least bit of significance in a democratic society is the one which occurs on election day. All we can ask of Canadians at that time, probably some three years hence, is to mark the report card. They are going to judge based on which party had some sort of concrete approach to the debt problem. Was it a party which, yes, did raise some taxes; yes, did put forth some spending cuts and some restraint proposals in an attempt to do something about it? Or are they going to go with the opposition parties which have nothing to offer but mindless criticisms?

speechtext: I apologize to the hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member for Edmonton West. The time has run out on questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I too, am pleased to stand in the House today to express my concern over the proposed goods and services tax, Bill C-62.
Lately the government has been playing the smoke and mirrors game by claiming that it is listening to Canadians and has thus brought down the rate of the proposed goods and services tax from 9 per cent to 7 per cent. The finance minister loves to tell us what a great guy he is for this reduction. However, he does not point out that he will make up the revenue he would have gained had it been 9 per cent by implementing other tax measures.
In other words, to help compensate for a revenue decrease of almost $6 billion, the minister plans to scrap income reduction for middle-income earners, reduce the refundable tax credits for low-income Canadians, reduce housing rebates, and reduce the indexation for family allowances and old age security. These are but four of the ways the minister will get back what he so arrogantly infers is money owed to him.
When each of the new highlights is added up, the total revenue for the government is $5.9 billion, or exactly what would have been made if the tax was introduced at 9 per cent instead of 7 per cent. Thus the finance minister will have taken the same amount of money out of the pockets of Canadians. It is simple math, and
Government Orders
Canadians will not be fooled. Canadians are not that dumb.
Here we are with a government that expects credit for saving $450 million by not doing something that it never intended to do in the first place. Canadians understand this tax, and they are loudly proclaiming that they do not want it.
The latest Gallup poll shows that 74 per cent of Canadians are opposed to the GST. We all know how much the government watches polls. Perhaps it should start listening to Canadians.
Canadians realize that the 7 per cent proposal is just as offensive as the 9 per cent proposal. Canadians realize that this is a tax faucet for the government. Once installed, the drip can and will be turned to full flow. In other words, the tax will easily get to the government's desired rate of 9 per cent or more.
Let us not get bogged down with proposed rates because this government has proven time and time again that it believes rates are there to be increased. After all, since the member for Etobicoke Centre became the Minister of Finance he has increased various taxes to Canadians 31 times. This is the same minister who termed the manufacturers' sales tax a silent killer of jobs because it damages the competitiveness of Canadian exports.
However, he has not hesitated to increase the rate of the MST on four separate occasions over the past five years. If the MST is such a great evil that it desperately needs to be replaced by the GST, then how could he justify these increases?
This does not say that I like the MST. I do not. I just believe that you do not replace a bad tax with a horrendous tax.
This proposed tax is everything the Minister of Finance promised it would not be during the 1988 election campaign. During that time the minister swore that he would not bring in a GST unless he had provincial co-operation. Well, he does not have that co-operation.
He also promised that any GST would be revenue neutral, visible and non-inflationary. It is none of these things. In fact, the Conference Board of Canada estimates that the rate of inflation will be between 1 per cent and 1.5 per cent. The government admits that this number is reached by taking a very optimistic view of the

February 5, 1990
Government Orders
effects of the GST. The Conference Board based these assumptions on those of the finance department.
The Department of Finance assumes that the savings of the cut will be passed on to the consumer. This is just a joke. There is no system in place to monitor such a move.
The minister promised Canadians that when he brought in a GST he would remove the 3 per cent temporary surtax on their incomes. He promised middle-income Canadians that he would lower their basic income tax rate. He promised business people that it would be simple to understand and administer. The Minister of Finance did not keep any of these promises.
Not only was the surtax not removed, it went up 2 percentage points. The income tax rate will not be lowered and the proposed GST will be a nightmare for the business community to understand and administer.
Most of all, the Minister of Finance promised that the tax would be fair. Canadians in every part of this country are continually pointing out just how unfair it is.
Is it fair that low-income families and persons living on fixed incomes, including seniors and welfare recipients, will be hurt by the GST? A senior with a given income will pay more, not less, taxes than his or her younger counterpart with the identical income. Sales taxes are by their nature regressive, simply because low-income Canadians spend a larger portion of their income on taxed goods and services than do higher-income people.
For example, according to Statistics Canada, families with incomes between $10,000 and $15,000 a year spend 92 per cent of their incomes on current consumption, with about 18 per cent of this being spent on food. In contrast, families with incomes of $50,000 or more spend only about 56 per cent of their income on current consumption, with only 7 per cent on food.
Although refundable tax credits are intended to compensate poorer families for the increased federal sales tax, many witnesses appearing before the finance committee were convinced that these increased credits would not fully compensate low-income Canadians for the added cost of the GST.
Is it fair that for the first time in Canadian history, books will be taxed? As was pointed out in discussions with the Nepean Library in my constituency, libraries will not be able to purchase on behalf of their clientele as much reading material because of this tax. As a result of the tax there will likely be less variety and selection of works for libraries to choose from because the booksellers will restrict their offerings to potential best sellers with less risk. At the very minimum, libraries will have the immediate impact of 7 per cent less money to buy books. This is at a time when the government is attempting to give the impression that it is fighting illiteracy.
Furthermore, by planning to tax reading but not gambling the government is saying that gambling is more worthy of support than the fight to end illiteracy.
Is it fair that the GST will wreak havoc on the tourism industry? One reason for this is that the GST discourages Canadians from spending their tourism dollars in Canada. This will have a devastating effect on the industry.
In addition, the GST will discourage foreign tourists from coming to Canada. Do we honestly think that these foreign tourists are going to save all those little sales slips and when they leave the country that they are going to turn them in for reimbursement? Of course they will not.
Is it fair that the real estate prices will increase and rents will rise because of the GST?
I realize that my time is getting short and my notes are not getting any shorter, they are still very long.
It is a real privilege for me to stand here because what I am hearing, not just in my riding but in letters from right across the country, is that people are very, very concerned about this. What it has shown me is that this government, as it has on so many other occasions, has failed the test. It is not listening to Canadians.
This government is tricky. It announces changes and calls them tax reform. Over all, the effect is to increase taxes for everyone except the well off. The GST represents a monumental shift in the way taxes are collected in Canada. Once that line is crossed there is no turning back.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, when the Federation of Independent Business states its opposition to the goods and services tax, it is because it does not understand or it has a vested

interest, whatever the excuse might be given by members of the government to support the GST.

However, the tourist industry states unequivocally that it is opposed to the GST. The stock answer for members opposite is that people do not understand. What we are faced with now in the House is an opportunity for the government to provide Canadians with all the answers and all the explanations. I am suggesting to the Minister of Finance whom I know wants to make sure that Canadians do understand his proposal that he should be speaking to the government House Leader, suggesting that all members of the House should have an opportunity to speak out in this forum and tell exactly what they feel so strongly about in terms of whether or not they support the GST or whether they oppose it.
Today I listened to the story on how the deficit problem in the country has occurred. Although it has doubled the debt, and the deficit is going to be well in excess of $30 billion this year, the government says it is the fault of the government that was in power 5,10 or 15 years ago.
If one wanted to look at it closely, one might want to ask what was the amount collected by the Government of Canada through the manufacturers' sales tax in 1984, what is the amount this year and what is the projected amount had the MST been left in force in the fiscal year 1991-92.1 think Canadians would be astounded to learn that in 1984 when this government came to power it was collecting less than $8 billion in the manufacturers' sales tax. Under the goods and services tax it will collect in excess of $25 billion.
It would be interesting for Canadians and for all members of the House from Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario who support the GST to stand in this House and tell us why they support it. Do not tell us why the opposition is spreading gloom and doom and that the opposition wants to take political advantage of the goods and services tax. It seems to me that it is

February 5, 1990
Government Orders
incumbent on members of Parliament to explain to the approximately 75 per cent of Canadians who are opposed to the GST why they are wrong.
The simple answer is for government members to muzzle the opposition. That is nothing new because of the experience of the finance committee over the past six months. As we travelled into Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina, Winnipeg, Elalifax, St. John's, Fredericton and Charlottetown, Canadians were given very, very limited opportunity to speak out as to why they were opposed to the goods and services tax.
That syndrome continues. The Minister of Justice came in this afternoon, rose on a point of order and told Canadians that not only would they not be allowed to discuss to any great degree the goods and services tax and what it means to them and their families, neither would elected members of Parliament. We will be precluded from speaking out on the goods and services tax. It seems absolutely ludicrous to me that people who believe in the goods and services tax will not stand in their place and explain to Canadians what the government propaganda machine and a couple of ministers who spoke out on the matter have been unable to do.
I was very pleased to learn over the weekend that the Minister of Finance will be attending a meeting of the chamber of commerce in Edmonton on March 5. Since there has been a coherent long-term approach on the part of the government to restrict appearances by government members to very special contexts, I and I am sure Albertans would like to see an open forum.
We would like to see a forum where not just members of the chamber of commerce but Albertans generally could attend, not to listen to a debate between two politicians, but to be able to ask questions that concern them. The problem with the GST debate so far is that there have not been many answers from the government except to suggest that we have to replace the manufacturers' sales tax.
I say to Canadians what they must ask their members of parliament who support the GST what the tax is meant to replace. The manufacturers' sales tax had raised less than $9 billion when the Conservatives came to power in 1984. The GST in 1991-92 is predicted to bring in in excess of $25 billion. That is a threefold
increase and the government says it is not a new tax. It may not be a new tax but it is going to bring in an awful lot more money than what was being raised by the so-called silent killer of jobs in 1984.
I would like to make a point to my western friends. Having travelled in the west, I know the deep-rooted feeling there against the goods and services tax. I would suggest that when members on the government side speak about the GST, and in particular about agriculture and farmers, they do not confuse the issue. The question of how farmers will operate their businesses in terms of inputs, credits, exemptions and so forth is one thing. It is debatable whether they will be better off or worse off.

They buy other things than what they need to farm with. That is why Albertans, Manitobans and people from Saskatchewan understand why this tax is bad. It is not just what it is going to do to the primary industries in this country, it is not just what it is going to do to farmers or fishermen, it is what happens when people do not understand that farmers, like every other consumer in the country, are going to be attacked by the goods and services tax.
Who's paying the MST now?

My friend asks who is paying the MST now. The people of Canada are paying the MST. There is no question about that. We paid $7.7 billion in 1984 but the Tories want to transfer a $7.7 billion tax that was being collected in 1984 into a $25 billion to $26 billion tax on consumers in 1991. That is the Tory way. That is the answer to the question.
Canadians know now that there is a manufacturers' sales tax and they know they are paying it. The fact is Canadians are saying to this government that they would rather stay with the status quo, the devil they know rather than the devil they don't know. That is what Canadians are saying.
The position of the Liberal party has been that we need to have tax reform with fiscal reform, something that nobody to the right understands. They know how to raise taxes. They knew how to raise them 31 times in five years, but they do not know how to practise fiscal reform

because they do not understand that the two go hand in hand.

John Diefenbaker, who I am sure you remember, had some thoughts on closure that he expressed during the pipeline debate. We are in this House today talking about tax reform, monetary reform, fiscal reform, and what do we have to do? Capsule it in five minutes or less because this government imposes closure on parliamentarians who want to discuss the GST thoroughly. We cannot as my time is ended because the government will not allow us to speak out.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously, in any society it is a lot easier not to make decisions, not to govern, than to try and govern a country. And when one does govern, one has to make changes from time to time, and it is not necessarily easy to do so. The same applies to bringing up children, because if we promise our teenagers a lot of things when they are growing up, and we are unable to keep those promises, we are stuck and we then have some difficult decisions to make.
The financial situation in Canada is not an easy one, and when we want to change projects or introduce new policies, people are going to raise all kinds of scenarios, and we have had examples of this daily. In fact, we saw this just five minutes ago, when a vote was called on a motion to extend debate after the usual time of adjournment. I have no objection to the principle, but don't you think that if we had not wasted our time last week on endless votes on the tabling of private bills, and if we had each used our speaking time, our ten or twenty minutes, instead of putting on this show to tiy and obstruct the proceedings of the House, there would be no need today to call a vote on extending the hours of business of the House.
There was plenty of time, except they had to put on a show, and we saw some incredible ones- I wish the hon. member would let me get on with my speech. I let you talk, now let me talk. I support the tax!
Last year, we had a debate on free trade, remember? You know what the Liberals said? With free trade, old age pensions will go. They said the same thing about tourism. Old age pensions, all that was going to go. That was a year and half ago, and it hasn't happened, yet. Monique Begin, former Minister of National Health and Welfare, said: With free trade, AIDS- You remember that one? And now they are trying to make Canadians believe any number of fairy stories. One thing is certain: this century saw a lot more Liberal than Conservative ministers of finance. In 1946, we had the Russell-Sirois Commission. In 1940, they took the Russell-Sirois Commission Report which had recommended to change the tax system and they shelved it. In 1956, they took the Carter Commission Report which had also recommended to change the tax system and they shelved it. Not to govern is much easier than to govern. That was in 1956. In 1966, they shelved also the Carter Commission of Inquiry report on taxation. In 1977, there was the Commodity Tax Review Group report. Again, instead of governing, they shelved this report. In 1983, they shelved the Goodman Report. There was one such report every decade, namely in 1940, 1956, 1966, 1977 and 1983. All these reports indicated that our tax system needed to be changed. Each time, the party in power decided not to govern and to continue as before. In 1984 or 1985, this Government tried another tack.
How did this develop? It was said earlier that taxes are not popular. It is clear they are not. We do not need surveys to find that out. Everybody knows that taxes are not popular and that governments try to get reelected. But how do governments go about it? When the needs are greater, they try to raise new taxes. If you were the prime minister of a country where religion forbade to eat pork, do you not think it would be easy for you, as a prime minister, to raise a special tax on pork? That is what you would do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: So let say it is forbidden.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It is forbidden. When something is forbidden either through religion or customs, people seem to jump on it. What did governments do 70 years ago when they wanted to tax people who were self-sufficient and
February 5, 1990

rich? They taxed manufactured goods because as a rule, people were self-sufficient, made their own fabrics, sofas, clothing, etc. Therefore, they levied taxes on luxury items because rich people had enough money to buy a manufactured sofa or weaved worsted clothes. This is how we developed our tax system in Canada. Because of the religious or historical context, we have had sin taxes-liquor, cigarettes, playing cards. Only recently have we been able to buy playing cards without excise stamps. And we started taxing the rich because the rich bought manufactured goods. So we said that was a good way to raise money. And we kept on doing it. Manufactured goods were taxed more and more, but there has to be a limit. It is not because one is rich that one will use a hundred times more manufactured goods than one's poor neighbour. There is a limit to that. It is not because I am rich that I will take 42 meals a week instead of 14. If I am rich, or if I have money, instead of buying groceries for my meals I will buy services, eat in restaurants. So, the more affluent I am, the more services I can afford. If I had money, why would I buy a $20,000 car? I would lease an automobile with a chauffeur! I would be stupid to drive. If I am rich, why would I buy a house? Why buy a house and look after the flowers? Instead, I will hire a gardener, rent a house, and so forth. I will rent services, and they are not taxable.
If tomorrow morning you receive $250,000 in interest on your investments, Mr. Speaker, just for the last three months, it would be stupid of you to invest them yourself. You would use financial consultants. Come now! The more affluent one becomes, the more services one uses. Fifty years ago, the more affluent one was, the more manufactured goods one used. It was tempting for governments to jump on that. But as everyone suggests, this is old-fashioned. Our Opposition colleagues also suggest this I think. They certainly do not agree with the proposal. But that is the direction the tax system will take. We simply have to propose changes.
I can see some Members who did not even bother to attend the proceedings of the Committee on Finance chaired by our colleague from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), so they certainly did not come up with meaningful suggestions. How do we go about it? Someone may not particularly favour 9 per cent, or 7 per cent, or even 5 per cent. We agreed to some exceptions. Some
Government Orders
people said: I would support a 5-per-cent tax without any exception. That is one option. The government chose another one. So now the government is facing the problem of taxing wealthier Canadians on what they chose to do with their money, and these are the people who now use ever more services.
Back in my riding I gave a few conferences on the GST and a lady said to me: Mr. Hudon, this means that when I eventually sell my house I will pay a 9-per-cent tax on the contract drawn up by the notary. I replied: Yes, Madam, you sell your house, the notary charges $1,000 for the contract, so you pay $90. You cannot afford to pay that? On any given day, do you know how many people sell their house? You will sell one in your lifetime. How many houses did you sell in your life? Two, Mr. Hudon. Do you know how many people sell houses every day? They are not taxed. What the Minister of Finance did through the tax reform is something new, at the same time a change in the income tax level and in the tax rate. This is the way we will improve our system, broadening the tax base and being more equitable by taxing rich people on what they do with their money. We are not hiding anything, Mr. Speaker. It has been suggested that people will leave Canada and that tourists will stay away in droves. Well now, the situation is the same everywhere.
The second issue to keep in mind and to point out honestly to all Canadians is that everything made or produced in Canada is subject to a 13.5 per cent tax.
We do not tell people enough-you are afraid to and some days so am I-that normally, the price of all manufactured products will go down 13.5 per cent and up 7 per cent.
Will the big corporations pass on the savings? We have to find some way to check into that. A system will have to be set up to do that. But normally, that is what will happen and what will help our exports.
We talked about it in the free trade debate. Canada, the Canadian economy, depends entirely on our exports-and I mean that. I do not get richer by selling something to my neighbour in Valleyfield; I get richer when I sell abroad and new money enters the country.

February 5, 1990
Government Orders
When our Canadian products are put on the market in Europe or the United States with a 13.5 per cent tax included, I am automatically disqualified or it is harder for me to compete for sales internationally.
Mr. Speaker, I say that if we want to maintain our social programs, if we want to maintain Canadians' collective wealth, we must bring money into this country and we will do that by exporting our labour and what we produce.
So I want to tax rich people on what they do with their money. Secondly, I want to make my exports competitive. Thirdly, and this is not said often enough, we have no external marks to distinguish rich and poor. I want to help the less fortunate deal with that expense. That is why there will be rebates based on the previous year's tax return. Households with incomes of $30,000 or less will get tax credits four times a year, not to spend the first day they get it. It is to help them deal with the extra expenses they will incur.
It is true that if they go to St. Hubert Bar-B-Q or McDonald's to eat half a chicken for $10, it will cost $10.70. We are not lying to people; we are telling them that is true. But to help them pay the extra 70 cents, they will receive a credit on January 1, March 1, July 1 and October 1. With that, they can handle the extra expenses.
We are not lying. I for one did not need that. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I am earning $80 000, and I do not need the rebate, I can afford it. One thing is certain-the Canadian economy will be paid for by Canadians, not by foreigners. The debt will be paid by Canadians, not by foreigners. It is our business. We are asking more and more from the government. Every year we used to pay all sorts of things for Canadians. There was talk about VIA Rail, about a lot of other services. We have taken firm action on the economy. There is a new Budget coming, and I am sure there will be more.
I remember in 1984, when we came up with our first Budget and started cutting, I kept hearing on the other side who is running today for the leadership of the Liberal party. She used to say: "Cut, Cut, Cut!" and "Jobs, Jobs, Jobs." Never so were so many new jobs created than since that time!
There are political risks to be taken. There are fiscal risks to be taken. And the risks we took in 1984,1985 and 1986 have borne fruit.
Mr. Speaker, as I said, I certainly want to tax the rich on what they do with their money. Second, I want to make our goods globally competitive by repealing the
13,5	per cent tax, and making our exporters competitive.
Third, I want to help the less privileged, because to them this will be an extra cost; those people I want to help face that new expenditure. And this, Mr. Speaker, leads me to the exemption. Not all goods will be taxed. Food will be exempt, drugs will be exempt, rents will be exempt, resale houses will be exempt.
So, Mr. Speaker, there are exceptions in-
What is the definition of "Food"?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: -Someone asked for the definition of food. The Liberals, Mr. Speaker, are wondering how to define food. Well, since they were in power for 22 years, they could have come up with a definition!
It's caviar and Big Macs!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Ah! Caviar! So that's it.. Here we go again, about those tons of caviar that are sold every year. The NDP and its crusade against caviar! Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are wondering how to define food. Shame, shame! So you really wonder?
Is barbecued chicken food?

You seem to have a problem. I suppose if I mention prescription drugs and tell them these are not taxed, they will say: What is the definition of a prescription drug? The people listening to us today, Mr. Speaker, can hardly be expected to take all this very seriously.
Mr. Speaker, the tax reform before the House today, which is part of the overall tax reform, will be beneficial to the economy of this country in general. All politicians are the same. They try to tax areas, not where it is politically expedient but where it makes the most sense to the public.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that tomorrow morning, the Minister of Finance will be able to sell Canadians a tax of
February 5, 1990

x per cent on all incomes in Canada for environmental reasons, because of existing public awareness.
That is what governments will try to do. That is what governments have always tried to do. Remember what I said earlier about farmers. Every country has developed its tax system in terms of historical, religious, financial or other constraints.
Mr. Speaker, we don't need polls to tell us that a tax is not popular. When I walk around-
In Chambly, too!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In Chambly, you've are got to be kidding it is not the GST which will get us elected or not. Don't worry! You can talk about Meech Lake in Chambly and show how much of a hypocrite you are but the considerations. They are totally different.
Mr. Speaker, they tell us that a tax is unpopular- When I walk down Victoria Street in Valleyfield, I know that the tax is not popular. But popular or not, Mr. Speaker, it is not going to make me change my mind. I am not here just to get re-elected. I am here to try to make some useful changes, to build a nation for our children and to give them the tools they need to succeed. Because the way we are going- And we all agree on this; there is no need for a Gallup poll.
Mr. Speaker, the way we are going, it will be an a tragedy if we do not give ourselves the economic tools we need to face the new Canadian realities and responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening with great interest to the hon. member for Beauharnois-Sa-laberry. I just did not quite understand his explanation as to why there is such a devastating percentage of Canadian people opposed to the GST.
I quote from the Star CTV poll just released last night which says that 79 per cent of Canadians are opposed to the GST and 16 per cent are in favour of it. That is not very many. Only 16 per cent are in favour of it. I think it is really the 16 Tories in the House tonight. These people are trying to muzzle Parliament by not allowing an extended debate so opposition members can explain to the government what is wrong with it and perhaps we can get some answers to these questions. Clearly, 79 per cent of Canadians are opposed to it. Only 16 per cent are in
Government Orders
favour of it and 5 per cent cannot make up their minds. I think they just probably have not heard of it.
In the member's province of Quebec the situation is even more devastating: 81 per cent are opposed to it while 14 per cent are in favour of it. I would think that it is not just what the hon. member hears casually when he goes back on the weekend, but people are really concerned. He simply has to get better answers and better explanations of why he wants to impose this dastardly tax on the people of Quebec.
Clearly in the west it is the same problem. Only 1 per cent more are in favour; 15 per cent are in favour there and 80 per cent are opposed. Some 5 per cent have not heard of it. In Atlantic Canada 16 per cent are in favour and 78 per cent are opposed.
I think it is important to note when we look at these polls that many people are not only opposed to it but are prepared to sign petitions, write letters to their MPs, attend rallies, vote against it, and boycott the tax. They want to take whatever action is possible.
I wonder if the hon. member could explain to the House why 81 per cent of the people in Quebec are opposed to it and only 14 per cent are in favour.

With the GST.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity tonight to return to the issue of the goods and services tax. On October 2 I pointed out to the Minister of Finance that the GST discriminates against the residents of the north.
Adjournment Debate
Because the cost of living in the north is the highest in the country, each northerner will pay more of this unfair tax. The public documents released on the GST do not mention the north.
I asked the minister why the north was omitted from the government's technical paper on the goods and service tax proposal. I also asked whether the government had done any background studies on the impact of this tax on the north and, if so, would the minister release these studies to northerners.
The minister replied that the government had done a good deal of work on the impact of the tax on the north and that the impact on the north is about the same as the national average. The minister said that the GST would improve the economic fortunes of the north by about 1.5 per cent. I was not satisfied with that answer.
My office followed up with the minister's office and asked for the studies and information the minister said he had on the impact of the tax on the north. We were told that it would take a little while to put it all together and that it would be sent to us in a very short time. It is now almost four months from the time I asked the question and we do not have those studies yet. Frankly, I do not believe they exist.
At the time I asked my question the finance committee studying the GST proposal had not put the Northwest Territories on its travel itinerary. I urged the committee to include the Northwest Territories in its travel schedule and a lot of pressure from the north was placed on the committee chairman to the same end. Eventually, that committee did go to Yellowknife to hear submissions on the GST, and it got an earful.
In a letter to the finance committee chairman the NWT Minister of Finance outlined the areas where the tax will adversely affect the north and other isolated regions much more than it will in southern Canada. He said:
The significantly higher costs in the Northwest Territories mean that northerners will pay much more under the goods and services tax than will other Canadians, while the proposed sales tax credit and other announced measures will be insufficient to offset the higher cost resulting from the tax.
It is the view of the government of the Northwest Territories that the GST will make the attainment of their goals of greater independence and self-reliance more difficult.

February 5, 1990
Adjournment Debate
The brief of the government of the Northwest Territories pointed out that modem industries operating in the north face some disadvantages that are not shared throughout the rest of Canada. Operating costs are very high. Labour costs are very high because it is more difficult to attract skilled workers and because living costs are so much higher in the north. Transportation costs are very high, especially in the smaller communities spread out across the north where all the goods must be flown in or brought out by sea lift.
These high transportation costs affect both the cost of consumer goods and the cost to business of shipping in its inputs and shipping out its production. The benefits to the NWT economy are extremely dubious.
What of the NWT consumer? While the sales tax burden on all Canadians will increase because of the new tax, the burden on NWT residents will increase by substantially more.
In 1985, prices for goods and services, excluding shelter, were on the average 44 per cent higher in the Northwest Territories than in southern Canada. With the GST, residents of the Northwest Territories will pay much more than other Canadians because prices are much higher to begin with.
The government of the Northwest Territories has calculated that if the current price differential still exists in 1991-and I predict it will be even greater-northern residents will pay over 40 per cent more in tax than southern residents. If the cost of housing is included the average price difference and tax will probably exceed 50 per cent because of the exceedingly high cost of housing.
Prices in Yellowknife are about 33 per cent higher than in Edmonton. But prices in some isolated communities, such as Grise Fjord on Ellesmere Island or Pelly Bay can average as much as 100 per cent more than in southern Canada.
It is the lower-income residents of the north who will feel the burden most. The sales tax credit will be much lower in real terms in the north and will not be high enough to compensate northern residents for the increased tax. Also, northern residents will begin to lose the tax credit at much lower levels of real income. For example, an employee in the NWT has to earn 50 per cent more on average to maintain a similar purchasing power to an individual living in southern Canada. An individual in the NWT earning $30,000 per year might
have a similar real purchasing power to an individual earning $20,000 in the south, but the southern residents will receive more of a benefit than the northern residents under the sales tax credit.
A further blow particularly affecting residents of the eastern Arctic and Baffin Island are Canada Post's new freight rates on food mail. These rate increases are averaging 20 to 25 per cent and will put some food out of reach for many families. A dozen eggs now costs $4.20. A litre of milk costs $4.50. These are the prices being paid now. These prices do not reflect what might happen to the cost of transportation under the GST.
The GST will apply to air fares and transportation. In my constituency there are no roads. Air transportation is a necessity. All our goods, food, clothing, hardware, and construction materials must be flown in, or they are brought in on sea lift in the summer months when the ocean waters are free of ice.
Under the GST fuel and electricity are going to be taxed. This will be a real additional hardship on northerners, where the necessities cost much more and where the consumption is much higher because of the climate.
Northern businesses will face administration costs. In the NWT businesses do not now have any sales tax to administer and accounting services are not available in many small northern communities.
The government has not considered how much harder this tax will hit northern residents; or, if it has, it has decided that it does not care.
When will the government recognize that the boundaries of Canada extend far beyond Quebec and Ontario?

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was disappointed by what my hon. colleague had to say. Right now, Canadian residents, whether they be northerners, southerners, easterners or westerners, all pay a 13.5 per cent federal sales tax.
And here was my hon. colleague talking about milk. We know that there is at present a 13.5 per cent hidden tax in the production of milk in Canada. Even on the carton itself and on the print on the carton, there is a
13.5	per cent hidden tax that Canadians don't know
February 5, 1990

about but still pay. What we propose is a visible 7 per cent tax on all goods, except on what my hon. colleague was talking about, that is food, which includes milk. Since the GST does not apply to milk, milk will cost less than it does right now with the 13.5 per cent hidden tax. We should not forget that.
On the other side, when we talk about the northern part of the country, we talk about mining, and about production. The 7 per cent tax is a consumption tax, it is not a manufacturers' tax or a production tax. So, in the long term, northerners will come to see that change of target as an advantage. In the long run, they will profit from that tax, and I'm happy for them.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the current
13.5	per cent federal sales tax, instead of equally helping all areas across the country, is in fact putting some of the regions, including the North, at a disadvantage, because, as you know, the system is 65 years old. It is outdated and needs to be changed. The new tax system will allow us to help all of Canada, and specially the remote areas, more than we can now with the current federal sales tax.
Mr. Speaker, I think that my hon. colleague would do well to examine the question in its entirety, although I know he has a special interest in the well-being of northerners. He would do well to put aside his partisanship, and to look at the real benefits the GST has in store for the people he represents and wishes to represent.
